Experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements in latency, hardware utilization, and energy efficiency compared to conventional fixed-precision and nonreconfigurable accelerators, validating TREA as an effective solution for real-time edge vision workloads.

item.title: Design of RF PAs With Pixelated Structure Assisted by Binary PSO Algorithm
item.description: A gradual evolution can be seen in the design methods for radio frequency (RF) power amplifiers (PAs) as artificial intelligence (AI) technology advances. Traditional design methods that rely on specific structures are being steadily improved by new approaches. In combination with intelligent technology, irregular structures have been used in the design of PAs to provide greater flexibility. A new general design method for RF PAs is presented in this article involving the combination of a pixelated microstrip structure and an improved binary particle swarm optimization (BPSO) method. By pixelating the microstrip lines into discrete regions represented by a 0–1 matrix, the matching network (MN) is made more flexible and efficient. In the initial attempt, the predetermined step-type matching circuit of the existing 0.5–4.5 GHz PA was pixelated in order to increase drain efficiency (DE) from 48% to over 55.8%. With a single pixelated microstrip line of 10 $\times $ 5 mm, an MN of the PA with a bandwidth of 2–3 GHz was designed without any predetermined topology. To extend the bandwidth, the input microstrip line was increased to 20 $\times $ 5 mm, and a 1.5–3.5 GHz single-ended PA was successfully designed, providing an output power greater than 40 dBm and efficiency over 60%. This methodology was subsequently applied to design a sequential load-modulated balanced amplifier (SLMBA), with a saturated output power of 42.7–43.18 dBm, an efficiency of 71.1%–72.13%, and a 10-dB back-off efficiency between 50.4% and 54.1%. In addition, all of the fabricated PAs undergo a modulated signal test using a 20-MHz 5G new radio signal, and excellent linearity is obtained after digital predistortion (DPD).

item.title: A 3.22-pJ/bit, 3.5-MF2 Modeling-Attack-Resilient Lightweight Strong PUF Based on Add-Rotate-XOR
item.description: Strong physically unclonable functions (PUFs) provide an exponentially large challenge–response pair (CRP) space for authentication. However, conventional single-bit-response designs must be evaluated repeatedly to assemble a protocol-sized response, increasing communication, latency, and energy overhead. Supporting wider responses reduces this evaluation burden but often involves elaborate transformation logic and substantial area overhead. This article presents a lightweight strong PUF architecture that supports 128-bit CRPs, aligning with standard cryptographic hardware interfaces. By leveraging add-rotate-xor (ARX)-based iterative mixing, the proposed PUF combines modular addition with carry propagation, bit rotations, and roundwise xor-based diffusion and entropy injection to achieve high diffusion, strong nonlinearity, and area efficiency. Implemented in a 180-nm CMOS process, the fabricated prototype occupies an area of 3.5 MF2, achieves a measured throughput of 202 Mbps at 0.8 V within the reliability-characterized operating range, consumes as little as 3.22 pJ/bit, and exhibits a bit error rate (BER) below 5E-7. Statistical evaluations, including the NIST SP 800-22 test suite, the NIST SP 800-90B evaluation, and additional analyses, confirm high randomness and low interbit correlation across the 128-bit responses, even under correlated Gray code challenges. Modeling attacks trained on 40 million CRPs show that the prediction accuracy is close to random guessing, reflecting the high nonlinearity of the challenge–response mapping and its resistance to the evaluated machine learning attacks. These results indicate that the proposed PUF provides an efficient and secure authentication solution for resource-constrained IoT systems.

item.title: Unifying Feed-Forward and Weight-Gradient: An Energy-Efficient Architecture for On-Chip SNN Learning
item.description: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) enable efficient on-chip learning but face a critical hardware challenge due to the computational asymmetry between small-kernel convolution operations in the feed-forward (FF) stage and large-kernel ones in the weight-gradient (WG) stage. Directly mapping these conflicting patterns onto a static architecture disrupts data locality, typically necessitating either disjoint processing units or redundant data movement, which severely compromises energy efficiency. This brief presents an architecture for unified learning in SNN (AULiS), a sparsity-aware accelerator supporting low-cost BFloat16 local learning (LL) via reconfigurable engines. Its core innovation is an algorithm-architecture codesign. We reformulate the WG stage into broadcast multiplications and map it to an output-stationary (OS) dataflow, newly applied to WG, complementing the weight-stationary (WS) dataflow used for FF. This strategy matches the distinct data-reuse characteristics of each stage: locking weights during FF and weight gradients during WG, allowing a single reconfigurable engine to process both, thereby minimizing data access and maximizing compute density and energy efficiency. Implemented in a 28-nm process, AULiS occupies 2.24 mm2 and achieves this unification with only a 3.4% area overhead. The architecture reaches 23.0 TFLOPS/W in inference and 22.3 TFLOPS/W in training, in dense-equivalent FLOPs at 95% zero sparsity. In a fair comparison, this represents a $3.78\times $ training and $1.50\times $ inference improvement in normalized energy efficiency over prior SOTA while delivering up to $10.64\times $ higher normalized compute density. The high and balanced efficiencies prove that learning can be unified with high-performance inference without efficiency compromise for adaptive edge artificial intelligence (AI).

item.title: SHAP: A Sparsity-Aware Hierarchical-Topology-Driven Ising Annealing Processor for Boolean Satisfiability Problems
item.description: Boolean satisfiability (SAT) stands as a fundamental problem that underpins a wide spectrum of electronic design automation (EDA) and artificial intelligence (AI) tasks. While the Ising model provides a powerful alternative for SAT solving, existing Ising-based solvers suffer from excessive storage overhead and complex mapping topologies. This brief presents a novel sparsity-aware hierarchical-topology-driven Ising annealing processor (SHAP) to address these challenges for 3-SAT problems. Benefiting from the proposed hierarchical Ising topology and its customized simulated annealing (SA) algorithm, the solving process is efficiently accelerated. Furthermore, by utilizing the hybrid coefficient management strategy, the memory overhead is significantly reduced. The proposed processor is simulated with a postlayout netlist in a 28-nm CMOS technology with an operating frequency of 200 MHz. The proposed design is validated using the SATLIB and self-generated dataset, with problem sizes of up to 50 variables and 218 clauses. It achieves a 97% solvability rate for 30–126 instances. While the benchmark MiniSat guarantees 100% solvability, our design delivers a $5\times $ speedup on successfully solved trials.

item.title: Glitch-Power Optimization Based on Effective Glitch-Source Identification and Holistic Glitch-Power Attribution
item.description: With technology scaling and design complexity increasing, glitch-induced dissipation has become nonnegligible in the dynamic power of digital circuits. In ASIC designs, glitch optimization is commonly realized through gate-level or netlist-level structural refinements, whose ability to achieve substantial power reduction with minimal circuit modifications depends on accurately identifying critical cells with high glitch-power impact. However, existing analysis methods misdirect optimization toward less-critical cells, because effective glitch-generation sources are not distinguished and glitch-induced power contribution is incompletely assessed. To address these limitations, this brief proposes a simulation-based glitch analysis and optimization framework. First, a waveform-analysis-based glitch classification algorithm rigorously distinguishes intrinsic glitch generation from propagation, resolving glitch-source misidentification. Then, the holistic glitch-power contribution (HGPC) attribution framework decomposes aggregate glitch-induced power and attributes both self-consumed and downstream propagation-induced components to effective sources, explicitly incorporating glitch-induced internal power ignored by conventional methods. Finally, a signoff-verified greedy engineering change order (ECO) gate downsizing framework validates the proposed analysis method in postlayout optimization. Experiments on several glitch-intensive benchmark circuits using 22-nm CMOS technology demonstrate average reductions of 32.9% in glitch power and 17.2% in total power, with only 11.08% of cells modified, significantly outperforming existing simulation-based methods.

item.title: 28-nm High-Consistency SRAM-CIM Macro With Cascode Current Mirror for Convolutional Neural Networks
item.description: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), neural network applications demand increasingly efficient data processing. The traditional von Neumann architecture faces a growing “memory wall” bottleneck, making computing-in-memory (CIM) a highly promising solution. This brief presents a 4-Kb 10T static random access memory (SRAM)-CIM macro designed for convolutional neural networks (CNNs), featuring a charge–discharge consistency circuit based on a cascode current mirror that provides stable bias voltages for current-domain computation. The proposed architecture significantly improves the consistency and linearity of bitline charging and discharging, thereby enhancing computational accuracy. Furthermore, only four tail transistors in the 10T SRAM bit cell are used to perform computation, greatly improving throughput. Implemented in a 28-nm CMOS process, the SRAM-CIM macroachieves an energy efficiency of 26.43–68.78 TOPS/W and a throughput of 1016 GOPS. With four-bit signed input and four-bit unsigned weight precision, the circuit achieves estimated inference accuracies of 93.4% on the MNIST dataset and 81.6% on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

item.title: A Low-Bit-First Multiprecision Processing Element for Energy-Efficient FPGA Implementation
item.description: Multiprecision multiply-accumulate (MAC) units from INT2 to FP32 are increasingly needed on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). However, the existing processing element (PE) designs mostly follow application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC)-oriented composition strategies. Their alignment and selection networks map to lookup table (LUT)-based multiplexing logic and incur rapidly increasing delay on FPGA platforms. We perform a controlled study of composition depth on three Xilinx platforms, spanning the Zynq-7000, Kintex UltraScale+, and Zynq UltraScale+ families. Each added composition layer incurs a steady frequency penalty, and four or more layers lose roughly half of the full-width maximum frequency. Based on this result, we propose hybrid high-precision composition (HHPC). The HHPC bounds in-array composition to a fixed depth. It moves residual high-precision assembly to postarray logic or inter-PE cooperation. It also preserves a fixed control structure across all modes. Based on HHPC, we implement a reconfigurable PE that supports INT2, INT4, INT8, FP16, and FP32 in a unified pipeline. FP32 is supported in two modes. A single PE produces one result every three cycles. A cooperative 3-PE tile sustains one FP32 MAC per cycle. On ZCU102, the proposed design achieves up to 310.60 GOPS/W for INT2 and 3.24 GFLOPS/W for FP32. It delivers up to $3.0\times $ higher energy efficiency than a comparable reconfigurable multiprecision PE with the same precision coverage.

item.title: A Low-Power Unified Swish and GELU Activation Accelerator for CNNs and Transformers
item.description: Nonlinear activation functions, particularly Swish and Gaussian error linear unit (GELU), have become integral components of modern convolutional neural network (CNN) and Transformer architectures. This work presents low-power unified non-linear activation (LUNA), a high-accuracy LUNA accelerator that efficiently supports both Swish and GELU activations using a unified datapath, and a piecewise-linear approximation based on the first-order derivatives of the activation functions, achieving high accuracy with low power consumption. Implemented in a TSMC 28-nm technology, LUNA achieves up to 80% and 96% reductions in area and power, respectively, with negligible approximation error at the activation-function level compared to prior state-of-the-art designs. Extensive evaluations on CNN models (LeNet-5, EfficientNet-B0, and YOLOv5) and a Transformer model (ViT-B/16) demonstrate that the proposed approximations preserve, and in several cases slightly improve, network-level inference accuracy relative to using an exact fixed-point (FXP) implementation. These results highlight the practicality and scalability of LUNA for next-generation deep-learning hardware.

item.title: An Energy-Efficient, Low-Complexity Parallel Stochastic Multiplier Using Partial Products
item.description: Stochastic computing (SC) is widely used in image processing due to its low hardware cost. However, it suffers from high latency caused by long bit streams. Although many parallel stochastic multipliers have been proposed, they are often complex. This work proposes an energy-efficient, low-complexity parallel stochastic multiplier (ELPSM). The ELPSM performs and operations based on uniform allocation, achieving high precision. The resulting outputs correspond to the summation of binary partial products (PPs) through shifting and concatenation. A unified formula is presented to design the ELPSM for arbitrary bit widths based on these PPs. Furthermore, approximate parallel counters (APCs) are utilized to optimize the ELPSM. Both the ELPSM and its optimized variants are formulated for easy scalability to higher bit widths. After optimization, the proposed multiplier reduces delay, power-delay product (PDP), and area-delay product (ADP) by 29.16%, 51.27%, and 50.78%, respectively, compared to a 32-bit binary multiplier, while achieving improvements of 18.81%, 32.33%, and 27.65% over the state-of-the-art 32-bit designs, respectively. The design demonstrates excellent performance in image multiplication and neural network inference; even the APC-optimized variants incur at most 0.45% accuracy loss on benchmark models such as ResNet-18 without posttraining.

item.title: A Bio-Impedance Readout IC With Phase-Locked Sampling for Real-Time Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy
item.description: This article presents an electrical bio-impedance (bioZ) spectroscopy integrated circuit (IC) that achieves both high-throughput and high-accuracy. The proposed phase-locked sampling (PLS) scheme, which employs a sampling phase-locked loop (SPLL) and a reference resistor ( $R_{\textit {REF}}$ ), enables fast and precise impedance demodulation. By extracting the impedance components through sampling rather than relying on DC settling, the proposed approach overcomes the inherent settling-time limitations of prior demodulation-based bioZ systems, thereby enabling high-throughput operation. In addition, the use of a reference resistor with the identical signal path of the target impedance allows effective cancellation of errors originating from the current generator (CG) as well as chip-to-chip variations in the amplifier and low-pass filter (LPF), significantly improving measurement accuracy. To further support wideband operation with low power consumption, the input signal is pre-demodulated to an intermediate frequency. This technique relaxes the operating frequency requirement of the readout IC, enabling a simple and efficient implementation of the sampling-based architecture. Measurement results demonstrate magnitude and phase errors of less than 1.78% and 1.8°, respectively, over a wide frequency range from 4 kHz to 2 MHz. Furthermore, the proposed IC achieves an input-referred impedance noise of 34.9 m $\Omega $ / $\sqrt {}$ Hz while supporting an output data rate (ODR) of 4–40 kS/s.

item.title: A High-Efficiency Multilevel Class-G Supply Modulator Using a Configurable Capacitor Array for Wideband Power Amplifier
item.description: This article presents a multilevel class-G supply modulator (SM) for high-efficiency wideband radio frequency (RF) power amplifiers (PAs). As the envelope bandwidth of modern 5G new radio (NR) signals extends to 200 MHz, conventional analog envelope tracking (ET) suffers from limited bandwidth, while switched discrete SMs face challenges associated with high system cost. To support wideband ET, a systematic design framework is developed to capture the fundamental tradeoff between multilevel voltage allocation and tracking rate. Based on this framework, a hybrid single-inductor adaptive-output (SIAO) architecture is proposed, enabling selective regulation of multiple output paths within each switching cycle and unified buck-boost operation. Multilevel output generation is realized using a configurable capacitor array (CCA) providing six voltage levels with three off-chip capacitors to reduce supply voltage overhead and the number of external components. A skip-charging constant-off-time (COFT) control scheme is employed to efficiently regulate the multilevel outputs under wideband operation. Fabricated in a 180-nm BCD process with an active area of 6 $\text {mm}^{{2}}$ , the proposed SM achieves a peak efficiency of 88.9% at 0.54 W and maintains over 80% efficiency from 0.3 to 1.6 W when tracking a 200-MHz NR envelope. When evaluated with a commercial PA, the SM improves the system power-added efficiency (PAE) from 6.2% using average power tracking (APT) to 7.1% at 19-dBm average output power.

item.title: A Nesting-Connected Reconfigurable SC Converter With Fine-Grained Conversion Ratios and Increased Output Conduction Paths for On-Chip Surround Power Delivery
item.description: This article presents a reconfigurable switched-capacitor (SC) DC–DC converter that achieves improved overall efficiency over a fine-grained conversion-ratio range, applicable to on-chip surround power delivery (SPD) in compact and lightweight devices. We propose a nesting-connected reconfigurable SC topology generation method, attaining fine-grained subdivision of reconfigurable voltage conversion ratios (VCRs) using a limited number of flying capacitors ( $C_{\mathrm {FLY}}$ s). We also propose a normalized modeling method to evaluate the steady-state conduction-loss property for the nesting-connected arithmetic progression (NAP) topology implemented in this work. Modeling results demonstrate that the NAP topology enables fine-grained VCR generation and improved fast-switching-limited conduction loss characteristics, compared with the conventional series-connection method. In addition, due to its inherent property of multiple output charge-delivery paths, the proposed NAP converter is suitable for on-chip SPD to achieve a more uniform conduction charge distribution. Fabricated in a 180-nm CMOS process using standard 5-V devices, the proposed SC converter occupies an active area of 3.432 mm2. It utilizes eight $C_{\mathrm {FLY}}$ s in 01005 packages, totaling a volume of only 0.128 mm3, to achieve 25 inherent step-down VCRs of this NAP topology, ranging from 0.11 to 0.67. Thus, the converter can convert a 5-V input to a wide-range output of 0.35–3.3 V. Measurement results demonstrate a peak efficiency of 92.34% at 50-mA output current and a maximum capable load current of 500 mA.

item.title: Verifica: Near-Memory Symbolic Interval Computing Formal Neural Network Verification Accelerator
item.description: Formal robustness verification of neural networks is essential for deploying machine learning (ML) systems in safety-critical applications. However, existing verification frameworks are predominantly software-based, incurring prohibitive computational costs and long runtimes, severely limiting scalability and practical deployment. Although symbolic interval analysis enables scalable over-approximate verification, its effectiveness is limited by excessive over-estimation introduced by non-linear activation functions, such as ReLU, and by inefficient data movement on conventional computing platforms. This article presents the first ASIC-based neural network verification accelerator that implements symbolic interval-based robustness verification through an algorithm–hardware co-design approach. The proposed method represents network outputs as a symbolic linear combination of input variables, enabling tight-bound evaluation via coefficient propagation. To mitigate ReLU-induced over-approximation, a linear relaxation (LR) with a tunable parameter is employed, along with an iterative ReLU state refinement mechanism that enables efficient adversarial example search when robustness cannot be directly certified. The proposed accelerator is implemented in a 65-nm CMOS technology using a transposable 10T SRAM-based near-memory computing architecture, allowing efficient interval arithmetic and symbolic coefficient propagation with minimal data movement. Measurement results demonstrate scalable and energy-efficient robustness verification, providing over 97% verifiability with verification latency ranging from 0.05 to 1.22 ms and energy consumption of 0.09– $2.14~\mu \mathrm {J}$ per verification. These results demonstrate that dedicated hardware acceleration enables practical, fast, and scalable formal neural network verification.

item.title: A Runtime Reconfigurable Array (RTRA) for Multiprogram ML and DSP Acceleration With Hierarchical Partitioning and On-Chip Multilevel Scheduling
item.description: Emerging applications with highly dynamic digital signal processing (DSP) and machine-learning (ML) workloads demand a hardware platforms that simultaneously deliver high performance, high energy efficiency, and low-latency reconfiguration. Such systems must adapt to evolving algorithms, variable data rates, and multiprogram tenancy without incurring prohibitive switching overhead. The conventional reconfigurable architectures and their associated scheduling frameworks typically rely on off-chip, software-based scheduling and mapping, introducing substantial latency and limited scalability. In addition, their dependence on the complex 2-D placement methods across processing-element (PE) arrays constrains responsiveness and resource utilization, making them unsuitable for real-time and multiprogram operation. To address these limitations, we present a runtime reconfigurable array (RTRA), a coarse-grained hardware fabric that integrates on-chip scheduling and is architected around modular, hierarchically partitioned compute blocks. This organization enables fast scheduling and mapping, sustains high utilization across diverse workloads, supports fine-grained multiprogram tenancy, and achieves high energy and area efficiency.

item.title: A Coherent Polar Phase-Tracking Receiver With High ACR and Relaxed I/Q Generation
item.description: This article presents a coherent polar phase-tracking receiver (PT-RX) for low-power Internet-of-Things(IoT) applications that supports Gaussian frequency-shift keying (GFSK), quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), and amplitude phase shift keying (APSK). Existing single-path closed-loop receivers achieve low power but suffer from a fundamental tradeoff between loop stability and adjacent channel rejection (ACR), and are generally limited to constant-envelope modulation. In addition, prior polar receivers rely on noncoherent amplitude demodulation, which limits their sensitivity and blocker tolerance. To address these issues, a delay- and phase-locked loop (D/PLL)-inspired feedforward phase path is introduced to create an additional loop zero, thereby improving loop stability and enabling stronger ACR in closed-loop demodulation. A coherent polar demodulation scheme is also adopted to improve the sensitivity and ACR of the amplitude path. Compared with conventional Cartesian I/Q receivers, the proposed architecture additionally shows improved immunity to I/Q mismatch. The proposed 2.4-GHz receiver is implemented in 65-nm CMOS and supports GFSK at 1 Mb/s, 16-QAM at 2 Mb/s, and 32-APSK at 2.5 Mb/s, achieving sensitivities of −86, −73, and −71 dBm, respectively.

item.title: A 108-Gb/s PAM-8 CTLE + FFE Receiver Front-End With 1.4-Vppd Input Range in 28-nm CMOS
item.description: This article presents a 108-Gb/s 8-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM-8) receiver front-end capable of handling a wide input dynamic range to overcome the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) versus linearity tradeoff in higher-order modulation schemes. The proposed architecture employs a multi-path continuous-time linear equalizer (CTLE) with a bias-shifting technique, which splits the input dynamic range to maintain high linearity even with a large input swing of 1.4 Vppd. To further enhance signal integrity without introducing non-linear distortion, a single-path shared feed-forward equalizer (FFE) is used. This FFE signaling path utilizes passive attenuators and track-and-hold (TAH) circuits driven by a custom 75% duty-cycle clock generator to ensure sufficient timing margins for analog tap delays. Additionally, a background statistical calibration algorithm based on output probability is implemented to automatically optimize the offset voltages for the sub-ranging configuration. The prototype was fabricated in 28-nm CMOS technology, occupying an active area of 0.255 mm2. Measurement results demonstrate that the receiver successfully processes 108-Gb/s PAM-8 signals over a channel with 10.7-dB loss at 18 GHz, achieving an energy efficiency of 1.95 pJ/bit.

item.title: A Single-Transducer Ultrasound System for Concurrent Power Harvesting and Adaptive Backscatter Communication in Bio-Implants
item.description: Bioelectronic implants have enabled precise and closed-loop interfacing with biological systems to diagnose, monitor, and treat disorders. A critical challenge for these chronically implanted systems is the design of a robust, real-time wireless data uplink and a continuous, efficient wireless power delivery link within a severely constrained form factor. Ultrasound, thanks to its advantageous path loss and safety limit, has become a promising medium. However, conventional ultrasound power and communication approaches either employ two separate transducers, resulting in a larger form factor or utilize pulse-echo backscatter with a single transducer, which suffers from time-multiplexed uplink transmission, limited data rate, and inefficient power delivery. This work introduces a single-transducer architecture that enables concurrent ultrasound power delivery and backscatter-based data communication, based on a unified impedance-based operating region that allows efficient downlink power harvesting and reliable uplink backscatter modulation simultaneously. The proposed single-stage power regulator modulates its input impedance via inductor charging-time control for data transmission while remaining decoupled from load variations, ensuring uninterrupted energy harvesting. The system further implements channel-adaptive modulation (BPSK, APSK, 4-ASK) to dynamically optimize the trade-off between data rate, reliability, and power delivery. Fabricated in 180 nm CMOS with a 0.28 mm2 core area and validated in oil at 5 cm depth with a 1 MHz acoustic wave, the system enables real-time data transmission and the highest spectral efficiency of 300 kbps/MHz with a bit error rate (BER) below $10{^{-6}}$ while achieving $192~{\mu }$ W of continuous power delivery.

item.title: A Scalable 1024-Channel VCO-Based CTDSM MEA Readout IC Achieving High Yield and Reliability Through Slot-Partitioned Channel Redundancy
item.description: Large-scale neural recording systems for in vitro bioelectronic interfaces require ultra-low noise, scalability to thousand-channel arrays, and long-term reliability to avoid chip replacement during biological experiments. This article presents a 1024-channel neural readout integrated circuit (IC) capable of both extracellular and intracellular recordings, based on a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO)-based continuous-time delta–sigma modulator (CTDSM) architecture. A slot-level channel replacement scheme is incorporated to improve system-level robustness against degraded or faulty analog front-end (AFE) channels, with potential benefit for manufacturing tolerance and long-term operation in large-scale microelectrode array (MEA) systems. Each slot integrates 32 regular channels and four spare channels, enabling faulty or degraded channels to be detected and replaced at the slot level, thereby relaxing the stringent single-channel yield requirements of large-scale neural interfaces. Fabricated in a 28-nm CMOS FDSOI process, the proposed IC achieves input-referred noise (IRN) of $8.06~\mu $ Vrms in the local field potential (LFP) band (0.5 Hz–1 kHz) and $5.34~\mu $ Vrms in the action potential (AP) band (300 Hz–10 kHz). After channel replacement, the measured SNDR and THD are 56.36 dB and 0.074%, respectively, with a total chip power consumption of 82.4 mW. In vitro experiments with cultured neurons validate stable multi-channel neural recording over several weeks.

item.title: A 96.7-dB-SNDR Two-Step SAR-Assisted Hybrid 2-1 MASH Incremental ADC With Automatic Inter-Stage Gain Selection
item.description: This work presents a two-step SAR-assisted hybrid 2-1 multistage noise-shaping (MASH) incremental analog-to-digital converter (I–ADC) that combines a hybrid continuous-time–discrete-time (CT–DT) delta–sigma modulator (DSM) with a noise-shaping SAR (NS-SAR) ADC. A two-step operation is employed to enhance power efficiency by disabling the CT stage during the second step (STEP2). A 4-bit SAR quantizer (QTZ) is reused across both stages, enabling a compact implementation. An automatic inter-stage gain selection (AIGS) technique is proposed to further enhance SQNR by adaptively selecting the inter-stage gain (ISG) based on the residue magnitude, allowing large ISG values without second-stage saturation. The resulting architecture provides second-order noise shaping in the first-step conversion and additional first-order shaping in the second-step conversion. Fabricated in 65-nm CMOS, the prototype achieves a 96.7-dB SNDR and a 100.7-dB DR for a 160-kHz bandwidth (BW) while consuming 1.61 mW at a 1.5-V supply and 16.64-MHz sampling frequency. The design achieves a Schreier figure of merit (FoMS) of 176.7 dB, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed architecture with the AIGS technique.

item.title: A W-Band Active Bidirectional Phase Shifter With 2° RMS Phase Error Over 26.4% FBW Using Back-Gate Biasing in 28-nm FD-SOI CMOS
item.description: This article presents a W-band active bidirectional vector-sum phase shifter (Bi-VSPS) using a bidirectional phase-inverting variable-gain amplifier (Bi-PIVGA) with back-gate biasing in 28-nm fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FD-SOI) CMOS. The Bi-PIVGA employs a neutralization technique that cancels the gate-to-drain capacitances of both active and inactive transistors in each signal direction. By using FD-SOI back-gate biasing, the Bi-PIVGA reduces gain-state-dependent intrinsic-capacitance variation, thereby maintaining neutralization accuracy and minimizing port-impedance variation over the gain-control range. This maintains I/Q accuracy and enables low rms phase error (rms P.E.) and rms gain error (rms G.E.) over a wide bandwidth in both transmit (TX) and receive (RX) modes. The Bi-PIVGA exhibits input and output return losses > 10 dB for all gain states above 71.5 GHz (TX) and above 71.9 GHz (RX). The measured peak gain is 4.7 dB at 93.5 GHz (TX) and 94.5 GHz (RX). Using this Bi-PIVGA, the Bi-VSPS achieves an rms P.E. ${\lt }~2.0{^{\circ }}$ and a maximum rms G.E. ${\lt }~0.34$ dB across 74.7–97.4 GHz [26.4% fractional bandwidth (FBW)] in both modes. At the maximum-gain state, the measured average gain is −4.3 dB at 92.1 GHz (TX) and 92.7 GHz (RX), with a core area of 0.21 mm2 and 80-mW DC power consumption.

item.title: A 138 Gb/s D-Band 2-D Scalable Transceiver Array With On-Chip Antennas Achieving Sub-1-pJ/b Efficiency in 28-nm Bulk CMOS
item.description: This article presents a D-band 2-D scalable phased array that integrates a $2{\,}\times{\,} 2$ transceiving (TRX) radio frequency (RF) beamformer with on-chip antennas (OCAs) and a $\times 16$ local-oscillator (LO) multiplication chain. The 2-D array scalability is demonstrated by tiling $2{\,}\times{\,} 2$ chips into an array using a low-cost package to build a 16-element hybrid array. The overall TRX system achieves >18% instantaneous RF fractional bandwidth (BW) and adopts a superheterodyne architecture with 10–40 GHz intermediate frequency (IF) range. The scalable chip occupies $2.115 \times 2.115$ mm2 and is designed and fabricated in 28-nm bulk CMOS technology. Dual-fed octagonal slot-loop antennas are shared between the transmitter (TX) and the receiver (RX) channels. The OCAs radiate from the chip backside after flip-chip assembly. Substrate thinning and substrate-mode cancellation techniques are applied to boost the OCA radiation efficiency to 33% at 140 GHz. The array maintains $0.45\lambda _{o}$ spacing between on-chip elements and $0.67\lambda _{o}$ between neighboring elements on different chips, which is limited by chip-to-chip spacing. The 16-element array module demonstrates a TX effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) of 33 dBm. An RX noise figure (NF) of 6 dB was measured over-the-air (OTA) using the Cold Source method. Beam steering was demonstrated up to ±60° in the H-plane and ±40° in the E-plane using integrated 5-bit phase shifters. This work demonstrates 138 Gb/s OTA using 64-QAM for the overall transmit-receive link while achieving an energy efficiency of 0.33/0.73 pJ/b in RX/TX mode. In addition, the link achieves a data rate of 108 and 72 Gb/s at 1 and 4 m link range, respectively. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this article demonstrates one of the highest reported array-level OTA data rates and the best energy efficiency (pJ/b) among other D-band arrays by a significant margin.

item.title: A 300-GHz 2-D Scalable 4 × 4 Phased-Array Receiver With Half-Wavelength Element Spacing in 65-nm CMOS
item.description: This article presents a 300-GHz 2-D scalable $4\times 4$ phased-array receiver (RX) with half-wavelength element spacing in 65-nm CMOS. To achieve high scalability, a hybrid local oscillator (LO)–intermediate frequency (IF) beamforming scheme based on a coupled oscillator array is proposed, together with an area-efficient aperture-coupled antenna implemented on quartz. The coupled oscillator array serves as a de-centralized compact LO source with low interference to the IF network, which is essential for enhancing phased-array scalability. In addition, it inherently provides phase-control capability, thereby reducing the area overhead of dedicated phase shifters. To guide the design of the proposed phase-control approach, the effect of nonideal LO phase progression in this scheme on beamforming performance is analyzed. The area-efficient aperture-coupled antenna employs a quartz superstrate with metallization on both surfaces. The slotted ground plane on the bottom quartz surface isolates the patch antenna from the on-chip circuits, enabling circuit integration beneath the patch and, thereby, improving phased-array scalability. The $4\times 4$ phased-array RX achieves a steering range of ±40° in the $H$ -plane and ±24° in the $E$ -plane. Measurement results show an RF 3-dB bandwidth of 293–307 GHz and a minimum noise figure of 23.6 dB. The chip consumes a DC power of 1.4 W.

item.title: A Quadrature-Rotation Phased-Array Transmitter With High-Resolution Phase Tuning and Complex Domain Power Back-Off Efficiency Enhancement
item.description: In this article, a four-element digital-modulated phased-array transmitter based on quadrature switched/floated-capacitor power amplifiers (SFCPAs) and reconfigurable switched-capacitor tuning lines (RSCTLs) is proposed. Phase shifting in each element is achieved by hybrid coarse and fine phase-tuning approaches. The SFCPAs with the quadrature-rotation technique are presented for coarse phase tuning. The baseband signals for the quadrature SFCPAs are preset based on the phase-shifting codes. Meanwhile, the RSCTLs are used for fine phase tuning. Capacitors with various capacitances are switched on under different phase-shifting states. To improve the efficiency at deep power back-off (PBO) peaks, hybrid Doherty and impedance boosting techniques are utilized. A 4-to-1 reconfigurable transformer is introduced in the SFCPAs for flexible impedance tuning. To improve isolation among four elements, active power dividers are utilized. The proposed phased-array transmitter is implemented and fabricated in conventional 40-nm-CMOS technology with a chip size of 8.32 mm2. The fabricated phased-array transmitter features a 28.4 dBm peak output power and 37.9% peak system efficiency. Meanwhile, 37.9%/33.7%/28.7%/23.5%/17.6%/12.9% system efficiency is achieved under 0/3/6/9/12/15-dB PBOs at 2.4 GHz. In addition, it supports 15-bit phase-tuning resolution with rms phase/power error of $0.12\boldsymbol {^{\circ } }$ /0.15 dB. For 25 MHz 256-QAM/40 MHz 64-QAM modulation signals, it exhibits EVM of 2.22%/4.69%, $\boldsymbol {P_{avg}}$ of 21.5 dBm/22.7 dBm, and average system efficiency of 23.2%/26.1% at 2.4 GHz. Utilizing a monopole antenna with a gain of 4.21 dBi, peak EIRP of 43.5 dBm is obtained. Meanwhile, the radiation patterns with $0\boldsymbol {^{\circ } }$ , $15\boldsymbol {^{\circ } }$ , $30\boldsymbol {^{\circ } }$ , and $45\boldsymbol {^{\circ } }$ beam steering are measured based on the monopole antenna array.

item.title: A Performance Comparison Between W-Band Sequential and Doherty Power Amplifiers for Power Back-Off Efficiency Improvement
item.description: This work presents a W-band sequential power amplifier (PA) featuring a compact and low-loss output combiner that enhances power back-off (PBO) efficiency by combining a main PA and an auxiliary PA through an isolated combining output network. The proposed architecture is analyzed and experimentally compared to the conventional Doherty PA (DPA). The analysis identifies the limiting factors for achieving 6 dB PBO efficiency improvement in DPAs and demonstrates how sequential PAs can overcome these limitations, particularly for high-frequency implementations such as the W-band. Both the sequential and DPA chips are implemented in a 16 nm FinFET technology. The sequential PA exhibits a small-signal gain of 13 dB over a 13 GHz bandwidth (BW) from 75–88 GHz, while the DPA achieves a similar 13 dB gain over an 11 GHz BW from 78–89 GHz. The sequential PA demonstrates better power performance, achieving a saturated output power ( $P_{\mathrm {sat}}$ ) of 13.6 dBm and an output-referred 1 dB compression point (OP1dB) of 13 dBm at 80 GHz, compared to the DPA $P_{\mathrm {sat}}$ of 12.2 dBm and OP1dB of 11 dBm at 83 GHz. Furthermore, sequential PA achieves 20% peak power-added efficiency (PAE) and 14% PAE at 6 dB PBO, corresponding to approximately $1.4\times $ efficiency improvement over an ideal class B PA at 80 GHz. In comparison, the DPA achieves 16.3% peak PAE and 10% PAE at 6 dB PBO, corresponding to $1.25\times $ improvement at 83 GHz. The sequential PA maintains this high power and efficiency across a wide 76–88 GHz frequency range, whereas the DPA exhibits a narrower operational BW of 79–87 GHz. The sequential PA occupies a compact chip area of 0.096 mm2, compared to 0.112 mm2 for the DPA. To the authors’ knowledge, this sequential PA achieves the highest efficiency at 6 dB PBO among CMOS PAs operating in this frequency band while achieving the highest efficiency improvement compared to class B PAs.

item.title: A −248-dB FOMref CS-Fusion PLL Architecture Combining the Advantages of PFD-CP PLLs and Sampling PLLs in a Single Loop
item.description: This article introduces a CP-sampling (CS)-fusion PLL architecture that combines the advantages of PFD-CP PLLs (robust and speedy locking) and sampling PLLs (low jitter/power) in a single loop. The PFD sends pulsewidth-modulation (PWM) pulses to a merged $\mathbf {G_{m}}$ /CP (GCP) block so that the phase error is represented by the PWM pulse during locking and the sampled voltage after lock. The locking benefit over a traditional sampling PLL relying on a frequency-locked loop (FLL) is analyzed and then verified via transistor-level simulation. The CS-fusion architecture is validated through two prototypes in silicon based on different types of PFDs and ramp generators, whose output delivers the sampled voltage ( $\mathbf {V_{s}}$ ) controlling the voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) in the P path, while also driving a PWM GCP followed by a loop filter in the mixed P–I path. The measurement achieves −253.3-dB jitter FOM ( $\mathbf {FOM_{J}}$ ) and −248.4-dB reference FOM ( $\mathbf {FOM_{ref}}$ ) while also attaining competitive locking cycles, with an average locking speed $4.3\times $ faster than the case disabling the CS-fusion technique ( $7.3\times $ faster if both without the aid of P path).

item.title: A Low-Spur Fractional-N DPLL With Analog Pre-Distortion DTC Implementing Second-/Third-Order Calibration
item.description: This article presents a low-spur, low-jitter fractional-N digital phase-locked loop (DPLL) employing an analog pre-distortion digital-to-time converter (APD-DTC) to suppress fractional spurs by compensating for both second- and third-order nonlinearities without using complex digital pre-distortion. To support background calibration, a spur-level detection scheme using phase detector gain (PDG) is proposed to adaptively update the second- and third-order compensation coefficients. This calibration requires just a compact 1-bit and one-entry lookup table (LUT), thereby achieving nonlinearity correction with minimal overhead. A prototype fabricated in 65-nm CMOS occupies 0.27 mm2 and dissipates 5.6 mW. With a 100-MHz reference and an integer-near 7-GHz output, the measured fractional spurs are suppressed to below −65.7 dBc, and the integrated jitter is measured at 154 fs. Compared with other digital PLLs presenting fractional spur levels below −60 dBc, the proposed design achieves the best figure-of-merit relative to reference frequency (FoMREF) of −238.8 dB.

item.title: Design and Analysis of Windmill-Shaping-Geometry Eight-Phase Oscillator Incorporating Magnetic and Dual-Injection Coupling Techniques
item.description: This article reports a compact millimeter-wave (mm-wave) quad-core eight-phase oscillator featuring magnetic coupling and dual-injection coupling. Specifically, the quad-core oscillator is integrated in an LC-ring configuration via a windmill-shaping transformer for phase noise (PN) and chip area reduction. The eight-phase oscillator could eliminate the oscillation mode ambiguity and save the power budget by exploiting a large transformer coupling factor. In addition, the inherent multiphase outputs are routed to the cascode tail-injection transistors to implement the dual-injection coupling. This act enables noise circulating and strengthens quad-core coupling that benefits the PN and phase accuracy simultaneously. Prototyped in a 65-nm CMOS process, the proposed eight-phase oscillator consumes 5.8 mW from a 0.55-V supply, scoring a PN ${}_{\text{@}{\mathrm {10\; MHz}}}$ of −129.3 dBc/Hz with the corresponding FoM ${}_{\text{@}{\mathrm {10\; MHz}}}$ of 189.2 dBc/Hz across the frequency tuning range (FTR) of 17.4% (20–23.8 GHz). Thanks to the windmill-shaping transformer, the quad-core eight-phase oscillator only occupies a core area of 0.07 mm2 with a superior FoMA of 200.7 dBc/Hz at a 10-MHz offset. The measured transient multiphase output waveforms exhibit a quadrature phase error < 1.5°.

item.title: A Versatile Laser Diode Driver With Dynamic Peak Current Regulation and Wide Tunable Pulsewidth Range for Adaptive Pulsed LiDAR
item.description: This article presents a versatile laser diode driver (LDD) for pulsed light detection and ranging (LiDAR) systems, featuring wide tunability in both pulsewidth and intensity to support a wide range of applications and dynamic adaptation across diverse ranging scenarios. The proposed LDD comprises three core components: a power stage with eight-unit cells supporting multiple current levels, a laser diode current sampling circuit for real-time current sensing, and a digital peak current regulation loop for adaptive current control. A unique peak current sensor is designed to capture the nanosecond-width and high-amplitude peak current, with careful design consideration for high-voltage operation. The proposed driver is fabricated in 180-nm BCD technology with an on-die laser diode and silicon/ceramic capacitors to minimize parasitics. The prototype is characterized under two setups covering low-/medium- and high-power operation. Measurement results demonstrate a pulsewidth tunability from 100 ps to 100 ns and a regulated peak current range of 3–22 A. Compared with state-of-the-art designs, this work achieves the widest tunable range and is also the first design that demonstrated closed-loop current regulation in optical transient measurement.

item.title: A 2 × 56 Gb/s Single-Ended Orthogonal PAM-4 Transceiver With Encoder-Based Crosstalk Cancellation and Linearity Calibration Techniques in 28-nm CMOS
item.description: This article presents a $2\times 56$ -Gb/s single-ended (SE) PAM-4 transceiver (TRX) with the encoder-based crosstalk cancellation (EB-XTC) technique, enabling 4-bit/symbol data transmission over a differential link. The EB-XTC scheme encodes two uncorrelated SE PAM-4 signals into a pair of seven-level orthogonal signals at the transmitter side and decodes them to PAM-4 at the receiver side, effectively canceling strong crosstalk in the closely coupled differential channel. To improve the linearity of the seven-level orthogonal signal, this work introduces a tailless push-pull (TLPP) driver with a linearity calibration technique in the bias generator, enhancing the ratio-to-level mismatch (RLM) to 0.96; moreover, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of decoded PAM-4 is improved by 15 dB. The proposed TLPP driver and orthogonal encoder leverage the nonuniform probabilistic distribution of a seven-level orthogonal signal to reduce signaling power. The prototype chips are fabricated in 28-nm CMOS and achieve 56 Gb/s/pin with crosstalk immunity up to −2 dB and SE insertion loss (IL) compensation capability up to 35 dB with energy efficiency of 1.8 pJ/b.

item.title: A 0.1514-pJ/bit 18-Gb/s/wire Run-Length-Tolerant Transition-Driven AC-Coupled Transceiver for Die-to-Die Interfaces
item.description: This article presents a transition-driven AC-coupled transceiver (TRX) optimized for low-power and compact die-to-die (D2D) interfaces. To address the limitations of conventional PMOS- and transimpedance-amplifier (TIA)-based receivers (RXs), the proposed RX architecture employs a small 130-fF coupling capacitor to capture only transition information, eliminating the need for bulky voltage reference generators (VrefGens) or high-static-current paths. DC levels are restored using PMOS and NMOS holders, tolerating long run lengths. The transition-driven inverter-based RX structure facilitates aggressive scaling of the transmitter (TX) supply voltage, contributing to significant power savings. A prototype chip implemented in a 28-nm CMOS process features a programmable three-lane on-chip interconnect with a 2- $\mu $ m pitch. The proposed design achieves 0.1514 pJ/bit and a figure-of-merit of 118.89 Tb/s/mm/pJ/bit, making it highly suitable for next-generation short-reach D2D interfaces.

item.title: A 27-Gb/s/pin Inverter-Based Delay-Matched PAM-3 Transceiver With Pattern-Selective Switching Jitter Compensation for Die-to-Die Interfaces
item.description: This article presents a 27-Gb/s/pin inverter-based delay-matched three-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM-3) transceiver for short-reach die-to-die (D2D) interfaces. The proposed design uses two parallel, identical offset-programmable transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs) to independently generate two finely tunable PAM-3 reference levels with minimal parasitic loading, enabling multi-level signaling within a compact, energy-efficient inverter-based architecture. A pattern-selective switching-jitter compensation (PS-SWJC) technique is further proposed, which selectively removes switching jitter (SWJ) only at switching-jitter events, thereby recovering the horizontal margin that conventional SWJ compensation (SWJC) schemes cannot restore. Measurements show that the proposed PS-SWJC improves the horizontal margin from 0.25 to 0.41 UI (a 64% enhancement) and maintains a stable 0.31-UI margin even with 0.94-0.95-UI peak-to-peak recovered-clock jitter under 60-Hz, 10-MHz, and 100-MHz supply ripple, demonstrating strong robustness to power-supply-induced jitter (PSIJ). These features make the proposed architecture a robust solution for high-density, low-power chiplet and D2D interfaces. The prototype transceiver is fabricated in a 28-nm CMOS process and achieves an energy efficiency of 0.399 pJ/bit at the DQ channel and 0.55 pJ/bit including the forwarded clock channel at 27 Gb/s/pin.

item.title: A 12-bit 1-GS/s SAR-Assisted Pipeline ADC With Gain-Stable Dual-Path Residue Amplification and Partially Look-Ahead Parallel Conversion
item.description: This article presents a 12-bit, 1-GS/s SAR-assisted pipelined ADC implemented in 28-nm CMOS featuring accurate residue amplification (RA) with low gain variation. A dual-path residue amplifier embeds an open-loop gain-error-cancellation path within the closed-loop amplification path, providing accurate gain and robust gain stability without additional timing or power overhead. Furthermore, a partially look-ahead parallel quantization technique removes the quantization delay from the critical timing path, effectively extending the RA time. Fabricated in a 28-nm CMOS process, the prototype ADC achieves a measured SNDR of 59.9 dB and an SFDR of 74.8 dB at 1 GS/s with a Nyquist input. It consumes 9.63 mW, corresponding to a FoMW of 11.9 fJ/conversion-step and a FoMS of 167.1 dB.

item.title: An Incremental Noise-Shaping Pipeline ADC With Single-Amplification-Based kT/C Noise Cancellation Technique
item.description: This article presents an incremental noise-shaping (NS) pipeline analog-to-digital converter (ADC) featuring a single-amplification-based kT/C noise cancellation technique. By pre-amplifying the frontend sampling kT/C noise onto the capacitive digital-to-analog converter (CDAC) of the backend NS successive approximation register (SAR) quantizer, the proposed architecture eliminates the repeated amplifications typically required in multi-bit SAR conversion employing conventional kT/C noise cancellation. Moreover, by preserving the residue information during the NS-SAR loop filter update, multi-cycle NS-SAR conversions can proceed continuously without additional residue generation. Together, these features allow multi-cycle multi-bit kT/C noise-canceled conversions to be performed with a single amplification, thus offering significant amplifier power and settling time savings. To further speed up the operation, two noise cancellation capacitors are rotated in a ping-pong fashion, enabling kT/C noise cancellation in the pipelined ADC. A variable-order loop filter is designed to enhance the conversion resolution. The floating inverter amplifier (FIA) is employed for both kT/C noise cancellation and residue amplification, with its linearity ensured through a two-step conversion and gain error calibrated in the background. Prototyped in 28-nm CMOS, the proposed incremental NS pipeline ADC achieves a 92.5-dB SNDR with a small input capacitor of 0.8 pF; it only consumes $467.3~\mu $ W when running at 1.6 MS/s, leading to a superior Schreier figure of merit (FoM) of 184.8 dB.

item.title: A 3.7 μW 93.5 dB-SNDR PPD-Based Noise-Shaping SAR ADC With Split-Capacitor Stacking
item.description: This article presents a pseudo-pseudo-differential (PPD) noise-shaping (NS) successive-approximation-register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter (ADC). A PPD-based split-capacitor stacking scheme is introduced to enable accurate passive summation. Compared to the conventional capacitor stacking scheme, the proposed scheme reduces the noise transfer function (NTF) sensitivity to parasitic capacitors. Combined with a third-order recycling integrator, the proposed architecture realizes a sharp and high-efficiency NTF. The dynamic-range (DR) degradation caused by mismatch-error shaping (MES) is mitigated through PPD-based prediction, even under input common-mode voltage deviation from the system common-mode level. Moreover, signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SNDR) degradation for differential input amplitudes smaller than the predictor and amplifier offsets is mitigated by intentionally shifting the input common-mode voltage. Implemented in a 180-nm CMOS process, the prototype ADC achieves a measured SNDR of 93.5 dB over a 1-kHz bandwidth. Operating from a 1.2-V supply, it consumes $3.7~\mu $ W, corresponding to an SNDR-based Schreier figure of merit (FoMSNDR) of 177.8 dB. The measured SNDR variation remains within 4.4 dB across an input common-mode voltage range of 0.2–1.0 V.

item.title: A 3072:96 Multiplexed Neural Readout IC With Two-Step Incremental-SAR Conversion and Efficient Bulk-DAC-Based Offset Compensation
item.description: High-resolution, large-scale neural recording from the cortical surface, using passive micro-electrocorticography ( $\mu $ ECoG) arrays paired with CMOS readout integrated circuits (ROICs), is fundamentally limited by interconnect bottlenecks. Emerging active multiplexing mitigates this; yet existing solutions often exhibit limitations in bandwidth and channel count. Furthermore, current DC-coupled recording analog front-ends (AFEs) suffer from degraded noise performance in the presence of large electrode DC offsets (EDOs). To address these challenges, this article presents a compact, low-power neural ROIC tailored for the acquisition of both low-frequency ECoG signals and wide-band cortical-surface action potentials (APs) from high-density active $\mu $ ECoG arrays. Employing 32:1 time-division multiplexing, our ROIC supports simultaneous recording from 3072 electrodes using 96 time-multiplexed channels (super-channels). To achieve high area and power efficiencies, each super-channel features two-step incremental-successive approximation register (I-SAR) conversion and embedded bulk-DACs (BDACs) for efficient EDO and comparator offset compensation. Fabricated in a 22-nm fully depleted silicon on insulator (FDSOI) process, this prototype neural ROIC achieves the highest channel count, the smallest effective per-channel area (0.0004 mm2), and the lowest per-channel power (438 nW), while maintaining a low input-referred noise (IRN) of 2.39 $\mu \text {V}_{\text {rms}}$ and 5.91 $\mu \text {V}_{\text {rms}}$ in the ECoG (1–300 Hz) and AP (0.3–7.5 kHz) bands, respectively. The ROIC’s ability to record multiplexed neural spikes has experimentally been demonstrated in saline.

item.title: A Single-Lead ECG Wearable Sensor With 1.04 s Latency for Cardiac and Biometric Detection Tasks
item.description: The wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) sensor has immense potential for cardiovascular healthcare monitoring. However, uploading ECG signals to server-side devices for diagnosis poses privacy risks. Multi-tasking ECG processors rely on multi-beat windows and complex models, leading to high latency and energy consumption that limit deployment in resource-constrained wearable devices. In this work, we present a single-lead ECG sensor for authenticated healthcare that performs QRS complex detection (Task 1), arrhythmia detection (Task 2), bio-identification (Task 3), and bio-authentication (Task 4). This sensor uses an invariant spectrum feature extractor on dual-mode single-beat ECG segments to derive normalized biometric features for these tasks, reducing the record latency to a single beat. A binary neural network (BNN) model is used for multi-task decision-making, achieving an accuracy of >94% across all tasks in the MIT-BIH database while reducing the model size to 5.725 kB. The sensor, implemented in 55-nm technology, occupies 0.50 mm2, with the digital processing core (DPC) occupying 0.27 mm2. Operating at a 0.85-V supply and 320-kHz clock, the DPC achieves a task latency of 1.04 s, representing a $2\times $ – $12\times $ reduction compared to state-of-the-art work, with inference energy of $0.19~\mu $ J/task ( $3.7\times $ – $26\times $ reduction).

item.title: A 0.38-pJ/step Pulse-Width Locked Time-Domain Wheatstone Bridge Sensor Readout IC for LIG-Based Wearable Strain Sensing System
item.description: This article presents a pulse-width locked-loop (PWLL) time-domain readout integrated circuit (IC) for wearable strain-sensing systems based on a laser-induced graphene (LIG) strain sensor. A time-domain Wheatstone bridge (WhB) architecture is proposed, incorporating a duty-cycled resistor (DCR) and a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO)-based integrator to realize a digitally intensive, energy-efficient, and highly accurate resistive sensor interface. A voltage-controlled delay line (VCDL) is employed to form the PWLL feedback path, enabling good linearity. In addition, a 10-bit delay-ratio-based pipelined time-to-digital converter (TDC) is proposed, eliminating the need for a time amplifier (TA). The prototype IC is fabricated in a 6-nm CMOS process, occupying an active area of 0.19 mm2 and consuming only 4.8 $\mu $ W. The system achieves high linearity with R2 > 0.99993 and a resistance-sensing resolution ranging from 8.5 to 4.1 $\Omega $ for conversion times of 0.1–1 ms, respectively, resulting in a figure of merit (FoM) of 0.38 pJ/step. Furthermore, an LIG strain sensor is fabricated and integrated with the proposed readout IC to demonstrate fast and accurate human-motion tracking.

item.title: Current-Locked-Loop: A Circuit Topology for Reconfigurable High-Accuracy CMOS References
item.description: This article introduces a circuit topology for building reconfigurable, high-accuracy CMOS current and voltage references, namely, current-locked-loop (CLL). The CLL regulates the $V_{\mathrm {GS}}$ of a current source transistor and thus its current output using a digitally assisted feedback loop, thereby enabling higher order temperature coefficient (TC) compensation and good reconfigurability simultaneously. By directing the current to an on-chip resistor, the CLL can be used as a voltage reference with a different set of digital calibration coefficients. Fabricated in a standard 180-nm CMOS technology, the prototype chip occupies an active chip area of 0.35 mm2 and consumes ~ $220~\mu $ A from a minimum 1.6-V supply. After two-point and batch calibration, it achieves ±0.027%/±0.056% voltage/current inaccuracy ( $3\sigma $ ) over the automotive temperature range from $- 40~^{\circ }$ C to $125~^{\circ }$ C, which improves the state-of-the-art by $2\times $ and $2.5\times $ , respectively. Moreover, the CLL provides a digital temperature readout with a $3\sigma $ inaccuracy of $\pm 0.06~^{\circ }$ C without further calibrations.

item.title: A Subminiature Light-Load Efficient Integrated DC--DC Converter Featuring High Inductance Density Bond-Wire Inductor and Low Quiescent Current PFM Controller
item.description: Integrated DC–DC converters, for the sake of small form factor, typically employ small-valued passives to facilitate on-chip or in-package integration. The crucial attributes of these converters for next-generation subminiature Internet of Things include low cost, small form factor, and high power efficiency. Achieving all of these attributes remains a formidable challenge for state-of-the-art integrated converters. In this article, we present an integrated DC–DC converter that concurrently achieves these three attributes by means of two innovations. First, a proposed high-inductance-density bond-wire inductor featuring a novel coil pattern leads to $\gt$ $ 110\times $ inductance-density improvement over contemporary bond-wire inductors. Second, a proposed low quiescent current pulse-frequency-modulation (PFM) controller embodies a proposed voltage-controlled-oscillator modulator and a proposed switched-capacitor zero-crossing detector. Owing to the novel modulator and zero-crossing detector, the controller features a low quiescent current of $\sim$ $ 65~\mu $ A, without compromising its very-high-frequency operation at 50 MHz. As a proof of concept, our complete integrated DC–DC converter realized in a $3\times 3$ mm2 package embodies the proposed inductor and the proposed controller. By leveraging the said two innovations, our integrated converter features low cost, subminiature form factor, and high light-load power efficiency. Compared to state-of-the-art integrated converters, our converter occupies a $\sim$ $ 40\times $ smaller form factor yet features $\ge$ $ 8$ % higher power efficiency at a light load of 50% voltage conversion ratio, from 10- to 50-mA load.

item.title: A Three-Level Dual-Path Hybrid Buck Converter With Mitigated Capacitive Current and Seamless DVS Across a Wide Output Voltage Range
item.description: This article presents a three-level dual-path (TLDP) buck converter tailored for mobile application processors (APs) with a 1.8-V input and 0.4–1.5-V output range. Conventional buck (CB) and multi-level buck (MLB) converters suffer from prohibitive DC resistance ( $R_{\mathrm {DCR}}$ ) losses in compact inductors as load current increases. Although various multi-path buck (MPB) designs have attempted to reduce inductor DC current ( $I_{\mathrm {L}}$ ) by supplementing output power delivery through flying capacitors ( $C_{\mathrm {F}}$ ), they are often constrained by restricted voltage conversion ratio (VCR) ranges and encounter severe efficiency degradation due to inrush capacitive currents ( $I_{\mathrm {CF,C}}$ ) at specific VCRs. In contrast, the proposed TLDP buck converter enables seamless operation across the full VCR range (0–1) while effectively mitigating inrush $I_{\mathrm {CF,C}}$ surges. Specifically, at the typical $V_{\mathrm {DD}}$ of 0.9 V, the proposed solution achieves optimal $I_{\mathrm {L}}$ -reduction and near-zero $I_{\mathrm {L}}$ ripple, thereby minimizing losses associated with the compact inductor and attaining superior efficiency. Fabricated in a 28-nm CMOS process, the TLDP buck chip delivers up to 2.5 A within a total area of 3.38 mm2, achieving a peak efficiency of 96.5% using a 1-mm3 inductor ( $L =240$ nH and $R_{\mathrm {DCR}} =24$ m $\Omega $ ). In addition, it attains competitive performance at the target VCR of 0.5, achieving an efficiency of 96.1% at 0.118 A/mm2 and delivering a high current density of 0.740 A/mm2 with 88.6% efficiency.

item.title: Building Minimum-Power Digital Circuits With Sub-Femtowatt Dynamic Leakage-Suppression Logic Standard Cells
item.description: This article investigates dynamic leakage-suppression (DLS) logic for minimum-power operation in digital circuits. The DLS logic family uses a strong intrinsic subthreshold leakage reduction technique and is an emerging approach for computing applications that prioritize low active power at or beneath the nW-level. We analytically model the key operating characteristics of DLS logic and show that a minimum-power point exists at an optimal $V_{\mathrm {dd}}$ that balances various sources of leakage current. We discuss available knobs for DLS logic and present a general design methodology for targeting minimum-power operation while also considering robustness. A fabricated test chip in 65-nm CMOS validates our models and design methodology with several unique DLS standard cell libraries, and measurements of traditional static-CMOS logic are included for comparison. Measurement results demonstrate a minimum DLS leakage power of 0.26 fW per inverter at 0.35 V, over $350\times $ lower than CMOS inverters at the same supply voltage. At 1.2 V, this leakage reduction increases to $\gt$ $ 1000\times $ . The library implementation of the proposed DLS libraries is validated with synthesized 8-bit DLS multiply-accumulate (MAC) circuits.

item.title: A 1.87-TELOPS/W 3-D Ising Machine for Accelerated Quantum Monte Carlo With Reconfigurability Using CMOS p-Bits
item.description: Qubit-based quantum annealing processors operate at ultra-low temperatures (15 mK) requiring enormous cooling energy. Consequently, there is a lot of interest in quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) algorithms that can be used to emulate quantum computing on classical machines. However, prior classical emulators implemented on CPUs, GPUs, or field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) are orders of magnitude slower than quantum annealers highlighting the need for dedicated application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Over the past decade, many ASICs have been developed, including general Ising solvers, typically implemented as digital system on chip (SoCs) targeting highly complex graphs, and specific Ising solvers, which address relatively simple Ising graphs using analog computing paradigms. General solvers often suffer from high power consumption, while specific solvers lack reconfigurability. This work presents, for the first time, a QMC algorithm implemented on a 3-D Ising computer fabricated in commercial 65-nm CMOS technology. Specifically, it solves a quantum problem in which a transverse field Ising (TFI) Hamiltonian is applied to an unconventional octagonal lattice. The reconfigurable integrated circuit (IC) also supports traditional 2-D Ising models for solving combinatorial optimization problems (COPs), offering better reconfigurability than prior specific Ising solvers. This IC achieved an energy-to-solution of $41.9~\mu $ J at 1 MHz and $16.65~\mu $ J at 10 MHz at 0.5 V for the QMC problem. Compared to previous FPGA implementations, this is a three-order-of-magnitude improvement and a six-order-of-magnitude improvement over CPU-based solutions. This article also proposes a new energy efficiency metric, $E_{\text {ELOP}}$ (Energy per ELementary OPeration), to better benchmark p-bit-based Ising solvers. Our IC achieves an $E_{\text {ELOP}}$ of 1350 fJ at 1 MHz and 535 fJ at 10 MHz (measured at 0.5 V) for solving the QMC problem, which are also equivalent to the energy efficiency of 0.74 and 1.87 TELOPS/W (ELementary OPeration per Second per Watt).

item.title: FSL-HDnn: A 40-nm Few-Shot On-Device Learning Accelerator With Integrated Feature Extraction and Hyperdimensional Computing
item.description: This article introduces FSL-HDnn, an energy-efficient accelerator that implements the end-to-end pipeline of feature extraction (FE) and on-device few-shot learning (FSL). The accelerator addresses fundamental challenges of on-device learning (ODL) for resource-constrained edge applications through two synergistic modules: a parameter-efficient feature extractor (FE) employing weight clustering and an FSL classifier based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The FE exploits a weight clustering mechanism to reduce computational complexity, while the HDC-based FSL classifier eliminates gradient-based back propagation operations, enabling single-pass training with substantially reduced latency. Additionally, FSL-HDnn enables low-latency ODL and inference via two proposed optimization strategies, including an early-exit mechanism with branch FE and batched single-pass training that improves hardware utilization. Measurement results demonstrate that our chip, fabricated in a 40-nm CMOS process, delivers superior training energy efficiency of 6 mJ/image and end-to-end training throughput of 28 images/s on a 10-way 5-shot FSL task. The end-to-end training latency is also reduced by $2\times $ to $20.9\times $ compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) ODL chips.

item.title: PANDA: A Reconfigurable Seizure Prediction and Detection Neural Network Accelerator for Epilepsy Monitoring
item.description: For effective healthcare management of epilepsy patients in a non-hospital environment, continuous monitoring of EEG signals is crucial, where wearable intelligent devices are essential. The existing seizure monitoring devices, however, cannot achieve high sensitivity, a short detection latency, a low false alarm rate (FAR), as well as ultra-low-power computing simultaneously. These devices also struggle to keep pace with the rapid iteration of seizure monitoring algorithms. In this article, PANDA, a reconfigurable seizure Prediction ANd Detection neural network Accelerator, is proposed. A lightweight, two-stage seizure monitoring framework with temporal neural network splitting (TNNS) is deployed on PANDA, which significantly reduces the amount of computations while maintaining high classification performance. An input channel first-output stationary (IFOS) dataflow, a zero activation skipping (ZAS) scheme, and orthogonal data reuse technique are employed to enhance the computation efficiency. A weight cache with statistical information (WCSI) is also proposed to minimize weight memory access. Furthermore, PANDA employs a custom instruction set, enabling the flexible deployment of various neural networks. PANDA is fabricated using a 65-nm CMOS technology and evaluated on two open-source datasets. For the CHB-MIT scalp EEG dataset, PANDA achieves 99.0% sensitivity, 0.47/h FAR, and 3.49 s detection latency. For the SWEC-ETHZ iEEG dataset, PANDA achieves a 98.2% sensitivity, 0.60/h FAR, and 4.61 s detection latency. Compared with the state-of-the-art designs, PANDA enhances energy efficiency by up to $5.49\times $ while maintaining competitive classification performance, providing a reconfigurable and energy-efficient solution for wearable epilepsy healthcare systems.

item.title: CTLIM: A 1.92 Mb/mm2 4T1C eDRAM Macro for Area-Efficient Cryogenic Ternary Logic-in-Memory
item.description: Cryogenic ternary logic-in-memory (LIM) is a promising solution to improve storage density and computation efficiency for data-intensive applications by performing ternary operations directly within memory. However, most previous ternary logic implementations rely on binary-encoded processing at room temperature, making it difficult to achieve the density benefits of true ternary operation for both compute and memory at cryogenic temperatures. To address this issue, this work presents a 28 nm $128\times 128$ cryogenic true ternary LIM (CTLIM) macro. First, we propose a compact four-transistor one-capacitor (4T1C) cryogenic ternary cell (CTC) capable of storing a trit, featuring a full-swing write path for stable ternary data storage and a decoupled dual-transistor readout for reliable sensing and efficient LIM operations. Second, we develop a true ternary write–read scheme comprising a ternary write driver (TWD), a charge-sharing-based bitline reference voltage configuration (BRVC), and a voltage-latched ternary sense amplifier (TSA). Third, we implement true ternary LIM operations, including one-operand [standard ternary inverter (STI), negative ternary inverter (NTI)] and two-operand [MIN, MAX, consensus (CONS), accept-anything (ANY)] ternary operations, enabled by the TSA and BRVC. Measurement results of our test chip in a 28-nm bulk CMOS process demonstrate that the CTLIM macro achieves a macro density of 1.92 Mb/mm2 and ternary LIM energy consumption of 23.63–31.27 fJ/bit at 77 K. Moreover, it also achieves a retention time of 18 ms, demonstrating area-efficient true ternary storage and LIM operations at cryogenic temperatures.

item.title: A Nonvolatile AI-Edge Processor With Lossless-Compressed-Computing STT-MRAM Near-Memory-Compute Macro Using Dynamic Floating-/Fixed-Point Accumulation
item.description: Nonvolatile AI-edge processors based on near-memory-compute (nvNMC) enable energy-efficient multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations with short wakeup latency for edge inference operations. Lossless compression is required for floating-point (FP) neural network (NN) models under on-chip memory capacity constraints; however, this imposes several challenges: 1) data decompression overhead due to lossless FP weight encoding; 2) a read-yield–energy tradeoff due to near-far effects in large nonvolatile memory arrays; 3) a MAC-accuracy–energy tradeoff in FP accumulation within the multi-level adder tree; and 4) inefficient layer fusion due to feature-map (FM)–weight mapping in nvNMC. This article addresses these challenges by presenting a nonvolatile AI-edge processor featuring four system–circuit co-design schemes: 1) delta-exponent lossless compression computation (DELC ${}^{2}$ ); 2) near-far-aware bias-and-mapping (NFABM); 3) dynamic floating-/fixed-point (FXP) accumulation (DF2PA); and 4) nvNMC-friendly hybrid-layer-fusion weight-mapping (CIM-HLF-WM). A test chip fabricated using foundry-provided 22-nm spin-transfer-torque magnetic random access memory (STT-MRAM) achieved an energy efficiency of 24.6 TFLOPS/W and a wakeup-to-response latency of 428.58 $\mu $ s under BF16 input and weight, verifying its effectiveness for capacity- and energy-constrained AI-edge applications.

item.title: A Dual-Mode TFT-LCD Driver Buffer Amplifier With Enhanced End-Point Bandwidth and Robust On-Wafer Stability
item.description: This paper presents a rail-to-rail buffer architecture for TFT-LCD driver ICs that addresses two practical challenges: bandwidth degradation near the supply rails and potential instability during on-wafer testing under heavy capacitive loading. Four auxiliary current buffers are introduced into the floating class-AB core to shorten internal control paths and maintain wide bandwidth across the full input range. To ensure stable operation with an 80-pF on-wafer load, the second-stage amplifier is partitioned and an impedance $R_{Z}$ is inserted to generate a left-half-plane zero for effective pole–zero compensation. In addition, a compact MUX structure with integrated ESD protection is co-designed to reduce the effective output-path resistance without enlarging switch devices. By redistributing the ESD resistance across parallel branches, the proposed design shortens the RC time constant and improves area efficiency. Fabricated in a 0.18- $\mu $ m CMOS process, the 20-channel prototype demonstrates stable, oscillation-free operation under 80-pF on-wafer loading and achieves 90% settling times of 346 ns (0.2–2.3 V) and 248 ns (2.7–4.8 V), with corresponding 99% settling times of $1.65~\mu $ s and $1.51~\mu $ s, respectively, under a 5-k $\Omega $ /400-pF five-stage distributed $R$ – $C$ load emulating a TFT-LCD data line.

item.title: Bifurcation Analysis Framework of Spiking Neuron Models
item.description: Neuromorphic computing targets energy-efficient event-driven information processing by placing artificial spiking-neurons at its core. Artificial neuron devices and circuits have multiple operating modes and produce region-dependent nonlinear dynamics that are not captured by linear system analysis methods, such as transfer function, Fourier/Laplace transform, Bode diagram, etc. Thus, new tools are needed to evaluate the nonlinear behavior of neurons and to guide the design and optimization of artificial neuron implementations. Here we present a generalized bifurcation analysis framework based on nonlinear dynamical system theory. A CMOS axon–hillock neuron, memristor neuron, and the Fitzhugh–Nagumo biological neuron model are selected for demonstration. We evaluate Hopf bifurcation conditions to define the rest and firing domains in parameter space of the system, and predict the near-onset firing rate. The results are further compared with numerical simulations. The framework standardizes the analysis for various neuron models and physical realizations. It yields practical design and optimization guidelines for artificial neurons for neuromorphic computing systems, including parameter combinations to make a neuron fire/rest and to control the corresponding firing properties, e.g., firing rate and amplitude.

item.title: A Sub-THz Dual-Tank VCO Using Active Negative-Conductance Boosted Architecture in 28-nm CMOS
item.description: This paper proposes a sub-THz voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) employing an active negative-conductance boosted architecture. The proposed architecture contributes to relaxing start-up conditions, improving tuning linearity, and increasing swing. A triple-coil coupled transformer is introduced as the tail resonator, simultaneously providing the broadband frequency selectivity of the feedback loop and further achieving conductance enhancement. The head resonator further improves phase noise (PN) performance while efficiently extracting second-harmonic components without requiring additional structures. And filtered output is achieved by a compact coupled-line-based buffer. Fabricated in 28nm CMOS process, the proposed VCO achieves a frequency tuning range (FTR) of 7.1% while operating at a center frequency of 109.6 GHz. At a 10 MHz frequency offset, the measured PN is -112.8 dBc/Hz, corresponding to a figure of merit (FoM) of -180.4 dBc/Hz. The VCO operates under a 0.5-1 V supply and occupies a core chip area of 0.035 mm2.

item.title: A 144-μW Phase-Interval Balanced RVCO With 142% Tuning Range and 218.2-dBc/Hz FoMTA
item.description: This paper presents a phase-interval balanced ring voltage-controlled oscillator (RVCO) with ultra-low power and ultra-wide frequency tuning range (FTR), for wearable or implanted brain-computer sensors. An approximate phase-interval error analysis model is developed to quantify the phase imbalance introduced by switched capacitors in phase-combined RVCOs. Based on this model, digitally controlled switched capacitors are incorporated into the low-power RVCO core to significantly expand the FTR while reducing phase-interval imbalance. An enhanced time-window phase combiner (E-TWPC) is further proposed to improve tolerance to residual phase-interval errors and mitigate phase noise degradation over a wide operating range. Prototyped in 65-nm CMOS, the proposed oscillator consumes only 16- $144~\mu{W}$ and achieves an FTR of 440 MHz-2.6 GHz (142%) under 4-bit digital control. This RVCO maintains comparable phase noise performance to existing RVCOs, while occupying a compact area of $0.00057~mm^{2}$ , achieving a $\mathrm{FoM}_{TA}$ of 218.2 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset.

item.title: A Low-Power Hybrid BJT--CMOS Voltage Reference for 0 °C--170 °C Operation
item.description: This paper proposes a low-power voltage reference that generates 736 mV over a temperature range of $0~^{\circ }$ C to $170~^{\circ }$ C, targeting low-power, high-temperature miniature sensing systems. Operating in the subthreshold region, a bipolar junction transistor (BJT) diode produces a process-insensitive complementary-to-absolute-temperature (CTAT) voltage, while stacked complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) transistors provide temperature compensation by adding a proportional-to-absolute-temperature (PTAT) voltage.
