Measurements from 76 samples across three wafers fabricated in a 180-nm CMOS process demonstrate a $\pm 3\sigma $ inaccuracy of 3.64% from $0~^{\circ }$ C to $170~^{\circ }$ C without trimming. The reference consumes 31 pW at $27~^{\circ }$ C and 113 nW at $170~^{\circ }$ C from a 0.9 V supply. Compared with the state-of-the-art voltage reference covering $170~^{\mathrm {o}}$ C, it consumes $4.36\times $ less power, achieves a 50% lower minimum supply voltage (0.9 V), and reduces the average temperature coefficient (TC) by $2.37\times $ without per-chip trimming (27 ppm/oC).

item.title: Distortion Cancellation in Asynchronous Sigma--Delta Modulators
item.description: This paper presents a design procedure for asynchronous sigma-delta modulators (ASDMs) that exploits distortion cancellation between the quantizer and the input path. By accurately matching the expansive nonlinearity of the quantizer to the compressive nonlinearity of the input path, the presented procedure relaxes input path linearity requirements, enabling power-efficient high-bandwidth designs. To support this procedure, a novel analytical model for first-order delay-based ASDMs is introduced that accurately characterizes the quantizer nonlinearity as a function of the loop filter corner frequency. Prior models assume a corner frequency much smaller than the self-oscillation frequency, limiting their applicability. The procedure is validated through the design of a 28 nm CMOS prototype. Operating at a self-oscillation frequency of 7.2 GHz, the prototype demonstrates distortion cancellation across a wide input amplitude range for frequencies within the loop filter bandwidth, while consuming only 3.1 mW from a 0.9 V supply.

item.title: A 93.5-dB SNDR 181.9-dB FoM MASH SAR ADC With Loop-Filter Noise Suppression and Mismatch Error Shaping
item.description: This article presents a multi-stage noise-shaping (MASH) successive approximation register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter (ADC) for high-precision and low-power applications. To achieve high resolution, a pole-zero-type MASH structure is proposed, which achieves a 22-dB loop-filter noise suppression and a 60-dB in-band quantization noise attenuation with high energy efficiency. A data weighted average (DWA)-assisted pre-comparison technique is adopted to suppress the digital-to-analog converter (DAC) mismatch while mitigating the input signal-range loss. A residue regeneration technique is also proposed to avoid the mismatched gain error across stages. Fabricated in 65-nm CMOS technology, the prototype achieves 93.5-dB signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SNDR) and 103.6-dB spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR) with 100-kHz bandwidth, leading to a Schreier figure-of-merit (FoM) of 181.9 dB.

item.title: A 15-bit 1-MS/s SAR ADC With Gm-Constant VCO-Based Comparator Achieving 181.2-dB FoM
item.description: This paper presents a high-precision successive approximation register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter (ADC) with a gm-constant voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO)-based comparator for enhanced energy efficiency. A cascode voltage-controlled current source and an isolation transistor are integrated in the comparator to stabilize the drain voltage of the current limiting transistor, reduce noise induced by operating region variations, and suppress kickback noise of the comparator to improve the precision of the ADC. The prototype SAR ADC fabricated in 65 nm CMOS process achieves a SNDR of 84.2 dB at a 1 MS/s sampling rate, while consuming only $100.5~\mu $ W, corresponding to a Schreier FoM of 181.2 dB.

item.title: A Low-Jitter Double-Sampling PLL With Linearity Enhanced Inverter-Based gm Cell
item.description: This article presents a double-sampling phase-locked loop (DSPLL) based on an inverter transconductance ( $g_{m}$ ) cell. A differential inverter-based $g_{m}$ cell with a constant- $g_{m}$ bias circuit is proposed to enhance linearity and suppress in-band phase noise (IBPN) without relying on a power-hungry charge pump or excessive reference buffer (RBUF) slew rate. In addition, compact duty-cycle corrector (DCC) and common-mode feedback (CMFB) circuits bias the $g_{m}$ cell’s input and output to the inverter’s trip point, ensuring the $g_{m}$ cell’s dynamic range with an additional power overhead of only $39\ \mu W$ . Fabricated in a 28-nm CMOS process, the prototype DSPLL achieves 53.6-fs RMS jitter and a −54-dBc reference spur at a 16-GHz output while consuming 17.3 mW. Measurement results confirm the loop maintains stable linear dynamics under reference frequency up- and down-steps.

item.title: Cryo-CMOS Integrator-Based DAC for Scalable Biasing of Semiconductor Qubits
item.description: Semiconductor-based cryogenic quantum processors require the accurate biasing of a large number of gate electrodes, which are typically individually wired to room-temperature DACs. To prevent the wiring bottleneck when scaling to future very large processors, this work proposes a scalable cryo-CMOS DAC that can operate with a S&H demultiplexer close to the quantum processor. By adopting an integrator-based switched-capacitor DAC with a dynamically-biased high-voltage output stage, both the required large output range and high resolution can be achieved while sharing the DAC over a large number of electrodes, thus improving the power efficiency. Fabricated in a 22-nm FinFET technology, the DAC occupies 0.076 mm2. At 4.2 K (RT), it achieves an LSB of $57.1~\mu $ V ( $68.3~\mu $ V) over a 3 V range with $188~\mu $ Vrms ( $192~\mu $ Vrms) noise and 36.5-LSB (12.6-LSB) INL while dissipating $157~\mu $ W ( $138~\mu $ W). The low power dissipation and the potential to drive more than 30,000 electrodes paves the way for scalable biasing of quantum processors operating down to mK temperatures.

item.title: Calibration-Free, Self-Referenced Thermal Control Circuit for Silicon Photonics Microring Modulators
item.description: We present a self-referenced, calibration-free control circuit for thermally stabilizing silicon photonic microring modulators. The technique monitors the through and drop optical output powers of the ring and locks operation at the point of equal intensity, a bias close to the maximum optical modulation amplitude (OMA). Unlike prior schemes that require reference calibration or external dithering, this method derives its error signal directly from the device outputs, enabling a fully automatic tuning. The all-analog feedback circuit, implemented on a printed circuit board (PCB), achieves stable operation for modulation up to 14 Gb/s with a response time below 1 ms, and a wavelength tuning range of 5.88 nm. The system maintains lock under ±6 dB input-power fluctuations, 1 nm laser drift, and $10~^{\circ }$ C ambient variation, demonstrating strong immunity to environmental and process variations. The approach offers a compact, low-power solution readily adaptable to monolithic electronic-photonic integration, advancing practical stabilization of high-speed silicon photonic transmitters.

item.title: A 220-GHz Transmitter Using IF Dual-Injection Mixer With High Conversion Gain in 40-nm CMOS
item.description: This paper presents a 220 GHz direct up-conversion transmitter (TX) implemented in a 40 nm bulk CMOS process with $f_{\mathrm {T}}$ / $f_{\max }$ of 300/270 GHz. To overcome the gain-limitation near the process $f_{\max }$ , a high-gain dual-injection active mixer architecture is proposed. By utilizing a compact triple-winding transformer and a frequency-selective network, the intermediate frequency (IF) signal is simultaneously injected into the gate and source terminals of the transistors with a 180-degree phase shift. A slow-wave shorted stub is optimized to behave as a half-wavelength resonator at the LO frequency to effectively short common-mode LO leakage and maximize the internal voltage swing. These mechanisms significantly enhance the conversion gain. Measurement results demonstrate a peak TX conversion gain of −8.6 dB and a 3-dB RF bandwidth of 15 GHz. The TX achieves a saturated output power of −11.6 dBm and an OP1dB of −14.6 dBm while requiring a low LO drive power of only −2 dBm. Consuming 26 mW, the transmitter occupies a compact core area of 0.2 mm2. This work demonstrates a solution for high-gain, low-power terahertz transmitters.

item.title: A 65-nm Multi-Modal Bayesian Inference Engine With 16.3-fJ/Sample Calibration-Free GRNG for Risk-Aware At-Home Skin Lesion Screening
item.description: We present a $65~{\mathrm {~\mathbf {nm }}}$ , risk-aware multi-modal Bayesian inference engine that enables privacy-preserving, fully on-device analysis for safe at-home skin lesion screening under uncontrolled user conditions. The compute-in-memory architecture performs in-word Mixture-of-Gaussian sampling, improving uncertainty fidelity beyond uni-modal Bayesian neural networks (BNNs). This added expressiveness increases equal-risk operating coverage by $\mathbf {1.4\times }$ , improves robustness to user-data perturbations by $\mathbf {\gt 1.5\times }$ , enhances process variation resilience by $\mathbf {5.5\times }$ , and improves balanced accuracy by $\mathbf {1.8\%}$ over state-of-the-art uni-modal BNNs. Hardware robustness is further strengthened by calibration-free Gaussian random number generation using complementary process variation, achieving $\mathbf {16.3}~{\mathrm {~\mathbf {\text {d}\text {J} }}}$ /sample and $\mathbf {168.6}$ GSa/s/ $\mathrm {~\mathbf {mm ^{2} }}$ efficiency. These results demonstrate a practical, energy-efficient, and risk-aware edge AI solution for privacy-conscious medical screening.

item.title: Reliability-Aware Behavioral Modeling of Automotive Safety-Critical ASICs With Response Surface Methodology
item.description: Automotive analog and power Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) operate over long mission profiles under elevated electrical and thermal stress that induces gradual transistor aging. In safety-critical systems, such degradation does not manifest as abrupt failures but as a progressive drift of circuit-level Figures of Merit (FoMs), which silently deteriorate safety margins. This work presents a circuit-level behavioral modeling approach for fault forecasting that translates transistor-level aging effects in power CMOS into safety-relevant FoMs—such as gain, switching point, and on-resistance—under realistic operating conditions, including supply voltage, temperature, and operating time. The model uses Response Surface Methodology-based Gaussian Radial Basis Functions and is validated on three representative automotive circuits with different degradation characteristics: a 30 V industrial high-side switch, demonstrating FoM-dependent degradation with some parameters remaining well within specification while others approach their limits under elevated stress; a 5 V comparator, illustrating subtle degradation across multi-stress inputs; and a 5 V common-source amplifier, exhibiting pronounced nonlinear aging and enabling validation of out-of-training prediction points. Across all cases, the model achieves 99 percent accuracy (coefficient of determination), while being lightweight enough to be deployed on a 20 MHz embedded processor, requiring only 1.6 kB of memory and $120~\mu $ s execution time.

item.title: HTR-Accel: An Energy-Efficient AI Accelerator With Hierarchical Temporal Reuse for Streaming Time-Series Signal Classification
item.description: Efficient classification of time-series signals poses significant challenges for edge intelligence systems in long-term health monitoring and real-time human-machine interaction. These challenges primarily stem from stringent requirements on energy efficiency, inference latency, and cross-user generalization. To address them, this paper presents HTR-Accel, an energy-efficient artificial intelligence (AI) processor tailored for streaming time-series signal classification. The architecture incorporates a hierarchical temporal reuse algorithm (HTRA) to minimize redundant computation, supports event-driven inference to suppress idle power consumption, and enables adaptive learning via fine-tuning for user-level model personalization. Implemented in 40-nm CMOS technology, HTR-Accel demonstrates cross-modal adaptability across four representative applications: electroencephalography (EEG)-based epileptic seizure detection, electromyography (EMG)-based gesture recognition, electrocardiography (ECG)-based arrhythmia diagnosis, and audio-based keyword spotting. Experimental results demonstrate that enabling HTRA in HTR-Accel reduces energy consumption per classification by over 85%, dropping to merely $0.12~\mu $ J for seizure detection, $0.36~\mu $ J for gesture recognition, and $0.15~\mu $ J for keyword spotting. These gains allow the accelerator to maintain competitive classification accuracy while delivering significantly superior energy efficiency compared to state-of-the-art designs, establishing an efficient, flexible, and practical AI hardware platform for next-generation wearable health systems.

item.title: A Computing-in-TCAM SAT Solver With Graph-Coloring-Based Variable Update and Dynamic Variable-Aware Clause Evaluation
item.description: In this work, we present an energy- and area-efficient satisfiability (SAT) solver based on compute in ternary content-addressable memory (TCAM). To improve computational parallelism, the variable grouping is implemented using a greedy coloring circuit that incurs only 8.1% area overhead. A dynamic variable-aware clause evaluation technique is introduced to skip unnecessary precharging operation, reducing power consumption by 17.86%. Additionally, a local charge-domain accumulation unit embedded within each processing element improves area efficiency by eliminating the need for explicit adder trees. The test chip is fabricated in a 65-nm CMOS process with a core size of 0.46 mm2 and operates at a frequency ranging from 50 to 200 MHz. Measurement results demonstrate that the proposed SAT solver achieves a 100% solvability with an average solution time of $18.19~\mu $ s and an energy consumption of 84.7 nJ, highlighting its strong potential for SAT solving.

item.title: ViTFCIM: A Sparsity-Aware Time--Frequency Computing-in-Memory Accelerator for Vision Transformers
item.description: Vision Transformers (ViTs) offer strong global modeling capability for vision applications. However, deploying ViTs on resource-constrained edge devices remains challenging due to the high computational and memory demands and the irregular sparsity. This work presents ViTFCIM, a hybrid Time-Frequency Computing-in-Memory (TF-CIM) architecture designed for sparsity-aware mixed-precision ViT inference. The architecture uses a Digital-to-Time Converter (DTC) to encode inputs as time-domain pulses and a Digitally Controlled Oscillator (DCO) to encode weights as frequencies. TF-CIM then performs time-frequency multiplication and in-situ phase accumulation in a multiplier-free manner. A data-driven time-domain sparsity-aware scheme is combined with an outer-product-based dataflow to adaptively skip ineffectual computations. Furthermore, a spatio-temporal bit-splitting strategy partitions input bits temporally and weight bits spatially across dual-SIMD processing elements (PEs), enabling bit-scalable operation. Post-layout simulations show that the 65-nm TF-CIM macro achieves a peak energy efficiency of 71.98 TOPS/W at 1.2 V in INT4 mode. Evaluations of DeiT-Tiny MHSA GEMM kernels show that the sparsity-aware encoding achieves average reductions of $4.22\times $ in energy and $1.89\times $ in latency. The mixed-precision bit-splitting scheme further achieves average reductions of $2.89\times $ in DCO-array power and $2.70\times $ in MHSA GEMM latency.

item.title: A High-Reliability and High-Performance Nonvolatile Magnetic Radiation-Hardened Latch Based on Approximate C-Elements
item.description: With the continuous advancement of transistor manufacturing processes, soft errors induced by space radiation particles have become a critical challenge in digital circuit design. This paper proposes a fully double node upset (DNU) tolerant nonvolatile magnetic (FDNUT-NVM) latch by using magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) and CMOS. DNU tolerance is provided by six cross-coupled PMOS dual-input approximate C-elements (PDACs) and a clock-gated three-input standard C-element (CG-TSC). Compared to the dual-input standard C-element (DSC), the PDAC reduces the number of transistors in the discharge path, thereby improving the speed and increasing the differential current. Furthermore, we propose an improved backup and restore module with higher reliability and lower power consumption than prior design. The proposed FDNUT-NVM latch achieves an optimal trade-off between speed and power consumption while maintaining high reliability. Using a physics-based STT-MTJ compact model and a commercial 40 nm CMOS design kit for simulations, the results show that under a tunneling magnetoresistance ratio (TMR) of 150% and a supply voltage of 1.2 V, the proposed FDNUT-NVM latch achieves a D-OUT delay of only 7.59 ps, a restore delay of 85.92 ps and a total power consumption of only $50.48 \;\mu \mathrm {W}$ . Monte Carlo simulations further reveal that the error rate of restoration (ERR) from MTJs is as low as 0.7%. Moreover, the proposed FDNUT-NVM latch can fully tolerate DNU even in the worst case with a deposited charge $Q_{\text {inj}}$ of $\pm 2 \;{\text {pC}}$ .

item.title: GS-Threads: An Energy-Efficient 3-D Gaussian Splatting Hardware Accelerator With Sparse-Aware Rasterization for Radiance Field Rendering
item.description: Real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) exhibits significant inefficiencies when mapped onto conventional tile-based rasterization, primarily due to the mismatch between anisotropic or finely projected Gaussian footprints and coarse rasterization tiles. This work presents GS-Threads, an energy-efficient 3DGS accelerator that exploits per-pixel sparsity via a Fine-grained Gaussian Rasterization Unit (FGRU). An $8\times 8$ Early Test Unit (ETU) performs $\sigma $ tests to generate hit bitmaps, while a shared Volume Rendering Unit (VRU) executes exponentiation and compositing only for valid pixels. Relative to a monolithic baseline, FGRU reduces LUT utilization by 56.6%, power by 28.6%, and rasterization latency by 32%-47% through sub-tile skipping. The design is implemented on a Xilinx ZCU104 FPGA with on-chip sorting and storage orchestration. At a clock frequency of 200 MHz and an $800\times 800$ resolution, GS-Threads achieves 116 FPS with 2.69 W FPGA Programmable Logic (PL) power (23.1 mJ/frame on-chip). Compared with prior FPGA-based 3DGS accelerators, GS-Threads improves throughput by 1.7– $2.4\times $ and reduces energy per frame by 2.3– $3.1\times $ . Post-synthesis ASIC evaluation indicates that GS-Threads achieves $1.5\times $ higher area-normalized throughput, and $1.3\times $ higher energy-normalized area efficiency than the recent 3DGS ASIC, delivering competitive performance–energy efficiency relative to existing hardware neural rendering accelerators.

item.title: A 28-nm Versatile TinyML SoC With Flexible Hetero-Fabric Dataflow Orchestration and Compute/Storage-Density-Adjustable CIM
item.description: Tiny machine learning (tinyML) brings machine intelligence to numerous extreme edge scenarios under battery-powered and always-on constraints, which imposes demands on tinyML processors for ultra-low power and versatile support for diverse applications and tinyML models. A heterogeneous-computing-fabric (hetero-fabric) architecture that incorporates compute-in-memory (CIM) core and multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit-based digital core (Dcore) can combine high energy efficiency and flexibility to meet such demands. However, the dataflow flexibility in the hetero-fabric architectures has not been well explored. Besides, previous CIM macros are limited by the inherently fixed compute-storage ratio, facing the dilemma of balancing compute and storage density requirements from shallow to deep layers in neural network models. This work presents a versatile tinyML SoC for diverse extreme edge ML tasks. Firstly, we propose a tightly-coupled hetero-fabric architecture for tinyML processing, where the CIM core (Ccore) and Dcore are tightly coupled through the reconfigurable data-streaming network (RDSN). Flexible inter-/intra-core dataflow orchestration for various tinyML models with reduced L1 memory access is further proposed. We also propose a layer-wise dynamic frequency scaling (DFS) scheme for hetero-fabric performance balance with adjustable inter-core clock frequency ratios. Further energy savings can be achieved when combined with dynamic voltage scaling (DVS). Besides, we propose a three-mode reconfigurable-LUT (R-LUT) CIM macro, which breaks the inherent compute-storage limitations and enables dynamically adjustable compute and storage density. A compact Twin-10T SRAM cell featuring lower read power is also proposed to construct the LUT array. Finally, we design a flexible Dcore featuring intra-core fine-grained workload partition and elaborate scheduling to coordinate with the Ccore for dataflow orchestration. The fabricated 28nm chip achieves $2.14\times $ higher SoC energy efficiency than state-of-the-art CIM-based tinyML SoC. It supports all MLPerf Tiny tasks, achieving practical performance (e.g., no less than 30 fps) with no more than 0.5mW power.

item.title: A 3-nm Aging Delay Characterization and Timing Error Resilience Framework for CNN Accelerators
item.description: As semiconductor technology scales toward the nanosheet node, aging as well as voltage and temperature variations severely degrade timing reliability in systolic-array CNN accelerators. Conventional guardbanding preserves correctness but incurs substantial performance and energy overhead. This work presents a fine-grained delay characterization of 3-nm MAC datapaths, revealing that timing errors are primarily concentrated along the sign-extension paths of high-order bits, thereby exposing the array-level delay frontier. Based on this observation, we propose an integrated timing-resilience framework combining a frontier-aligned timing monitor and a hybrid mitigation scheme. The placement-aware monitor tracks the worst-case delay frontier with only 1.75% average estimation error, while adaptive MSB sign-bit recovery and LSB truncation effectively suppress accuracy degradation. Under the most severe aging, the proposed framework maintains 97.7% LeNet-5 accuracy, compared with 10.9% for the baseline. Implemented on a $16\times 16$ systolic array, the design incurs only 2.8% area overhead and improves power efficiency under both fresh and aged conditions without sacrificing accuracy. Additional RTL-level evaluations across CNN models of different sizes, including AlexNet, VGG11, and ResNet18, further demonstrate the scalability of the proposed mitigation strategy.

item.title: A 28-nm Soft Error Tolerant SRAM With Design-Layout Co-Optimized 14T Cell and Double Mode Redundant Peripheral Circuit for Space Application
item.description: This work presents a radiation-hardened 28 nm SRAM with Design-Layout Co-Optimized 14T cell (DLCO-14T) and double mode redundant peripheral circuit for space applications. The proposed architecture exhibits strong resilience to single-event effects (SEE), withstanding laser irradiation at a linear energy transfer (LET) of up to 60 MeV $\cdot $ cm2/mg. The memory cell achieves a normalized critical path distance (NCPD) of 67%, approximately twice that of conventional rad-hard designs. By integrating a dual-mode decoding strategy, dual-port cell configuration, and a DICE-latched sense amplifier (DL-SA), the SRAM remains functional at operating frequencies above 500 MHz under radiation. A mixed-mode redundancy (MMR) delay chain in the sense amplifier control circuitry achieves single-event transient (SET) immunity with an area overhead of 140%. Experiment results confirm no failure at laser injecting at hardened zone and an 87.9% soft error rate reduction at laser injecting at non-hardened zone, demonstrating high reliability for space systems.

item.title: An Energy-Efficient Channel-Wise Segmented Sparse BNN Accelerator With Algorithm--Hardware Co-Optimization for Gesture Recognition
item.description: This paper presents an energy-efficient channel-wise segmented sparse binarized neural network accelerator (SBNA) via algorithm-hardware co-optimization for real-time gesture recognition. At the algorithm level, a novel channel-wise segmented sparse binarized neural network (SSBNN) is proposed to fundamentally addresses the inefficiency of pruning sparsity in BNN by introducing structured segmented activation sparsity. We adopt a channel-level positive-or-negative ratio loss to naturally induce hardware-friendly sparse patterns during training, grouping sparse data into segmented sparse activation vectors for efficient compression and computation. At the hardware level, our SBNA is designed to fully exploits algorithmic sparsity through three synergistic architectural innovations: 1) a Channel Shuffled Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) Compression Unit (CSCSRCU) that strategically integrates channel shuffling with CSR encoding to maximize compression efficiency; 2) a Sparse-Aware Value Prediction Unit (SAVPU) that intelligently leverages segmented sparsity patterns to eliminate redundant MAC operations with minimal memory overhead; and 3) a Greedy Computation Scheduler (GCS) that dynamically optimizes processing element utilization by aligning computation scheduling with the intrinsic sparsity structure. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SSBNN achieves 85.52-96.37% sparsity in activation maps except first layer and fully connected layers, and 89.32-98.62% accuracy with only $\le 29.55$ million operations (MOP) and $\le 18.33$ KB of parameters across gesture datasets. The CSCSRCU achieves a compression ratio of 2.46- $3.85\times $ with 1.22- $1.73\times $ higher compression efficiency than CSR-only compression. The SAVPU reduces multiply-accumulate operations by 85.52-96.37% using a minimal overhead of 1.375 KB on-chip buffer, while the GCS reduces inference latency by 3.19- $4.18\times $ . Our SBNA achieves 8.16- $10.72~\mu $ s latency, 3.082 W power consumption, and 894.09 - 1174.56 GOPS/W energy efficiency at 50 MHz on an embedded FPGA, delivering superior performance compared to state-of-the-art gesture recognition accelerators.

item.title: A High-Linearity Hybrid-Domain SRAM-CIM Macro With Wide-Margin Voltage-to-Time Interface and Process-Adaptive TDC
item.description: SRAM-based computing-in-memory (SRAM-CIM) alleviates the memory-wall bottleneck of the von Neumann architecture, enabling energy-efficient AI edge computing. Current-domain CIM schemes suffer from degraded linearity at low supply voltages, whereas time-domain CIM schemes are highly sensitive to process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variations. This paper presents a hybrid-domain SRAM-CIM macro featuring enhanced linearity and process-adaptive quantization. Specifically, a current mirror discharge and inverting Schmitt trigger (CMD-IS) module converts bit-line voltage-signals into time-signals, alleviating discharge nonlinearity while ensuring a uniform slew rate. Additionally, guided by statistical analysis of the column-wise multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) value probability distribution, a resolution-tunable stepwise-encoded time-to-digital converter (RTSE TDC) reduces quantization overhead, while a process corner detection and delay regulation (PDDR) module adaptively calibrates TDC quantization steps to compensate for process corner variations. Implemented in 28 nm CMOS technology, the macro achieves peak energy efficiencies of 29.88 TOPS/W and 36.88 TOPS/W in signed and unsigned CIM modes, respectively, with area efficiencies of 6.00 TOPS/mm2 and 5.88 TOPS/mm2. For the ResNet-20@CIFAR-10 and ResNet-20@CIFAR-100 datasets, the macro achieves inference accuracies of 91.33% and 67.43%.

item.title: HiKV: Hierarchical Importance-Aware KV Cache With Hardware Acceleration for LLM Decoding
item.description: With the rapid adoption of long-context large language models (LLMs), the continuously growing KV cache during decoding has become the critical memory bottleneck. To tackle this challenge, we propose HiKV, a novel algorithm-hardware co-design that exploits KV cache redundancy through hierarchical importance awareness. Algorithmically, HiKV compresses the KV cache at two granularities: Stage I evicts unimportant tokens within a fixed budget, and Stage II further loads only the significant elements of each retained token, reaching compression ratios unattainable at a single granularity. Architecturally, we develop a dedicated accelerator centered on a reconfigurable importance sorter that switches between the distinct sorting datapaths each stage requires, unifying the two-stage acceleration in one circuit with minimal overhead. Evaluated on representative LLMs, HiKV achieves up to 7.95 $\times $ speedup and 90% energy reduction in the attention computation over the vanilla KV cache baseline within negligible 1% accuracy loss. Under iso-accuracy constraints, HiKV outperforms state-of-the-art importance-based methods by achieving an additional $1.82\sim 4.87\times $ reduction in external memory accesses. These benefits are enabled by specialized hardware components that add only 8% to the system area.

item.title: BoMa-MAC: A Boolean-Masked Multiply-Accumulate Unit for Secure DNN Accelerators
item.description: With the deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) at the edge, the side-channel security of hardware accelerators has become increasingly critical. As the dominant computational primitive, the multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit directly processes sensitive model parameters and therefore constitutes a critical attack target. Although masking is an effective countermeasure against side-channel attacks (SCAs), existing protected DNN designs either rely on circuit-specific optimizations or compose masked multipliers and adders separately, limiting their generality, scalability, and throughput. This paper proposes BoMa-MAC, a Boolean-masked MAC architecture for multi-bit fixed-point DNN accelerators. Based on a modified Baugh–Wooley algorithm, BoMa-MAC restructures signed multiplication and accumulation into a unified security-oriented array MAC datapath. It further introduces multiple dedicated masked computational gadgets designed for the array MAC structure, using the domain-oriented masking (DOM) AND gate as the secure nonlinear primitive. A structured randomness-reuse strategy and a deeply pipelined architecture are also developed to support scalable and high-throughput masked execution. The proposed design achieves first-order security under the glitch-extended probing model. Building on the INT8 BoMa-MAC, we construct secure 1-D and 2-D systolic arrays and evaluate their security, scalability, and performance. FPGA implementation results show overheads of $5\times $ in lookup tables (LUTs), $3.7\times $ in flip-flops (FFs), and $1.6\times $ in setup latency, while preserving one output per cycle after pipeline filling. TVLA and CPA evaluations using up to 1M power traces validate the first-order side-channel resistance of BoMa-MAC and its systolic-array integrations.

item.title: TEF-CIM: Heterogeneous Tri-Flow Training CIM Macro With Exponent-Exclusive Addend-Compression and Adder-Free Arithmetic Enabling Fused Weight Update
item.description: This article reports a heterogeneous tri-flow compute-in-memory (TEF-CIM) macro that enables end-to-end edge DNN training operations, including forward propagation, error backpropagation (EBP), weight gradient calculation (WGC), and weight update (WU). It features several techniques that enhance the area/energy efficiency and reduce the external memory access: 1) a bit-polarity-interleaved 4T/12T/14T addend-compression matrix-vector-multiplication (MVM) CIM core with complementary 5T-SRAM for hardware-efficient exponent-exclusive 8b (EF8) operation; 2) A vector-outer-product (VOP) CIM core with adder-free bit-select SRAM signed ripple counter, reducing the partial sum access of WGC by $37.3\times $ in ResNet-50; 3) a heterogeneous tri-flow data loading system fusing EBP, WGC, and WU, which reduces the total external memory access by $2.7\times $ in ResNet-50. The proposed TEF-CIM macro prototyped in 28-nm CMOS reaches a peak energy efficiency of 208.6 TFLOPS/W, and an area efficiency of 3.81 TFLOPS/mm2.

item.title: Small-Area and Low-Power Fallback Unit Based on Hybridization of Recurrence Relations and Efficient Dual Modular Redundancy for NTT/INTT
item.description: In this paper, a special component named fallback unit (FBU) is presented for the number theoretic transform (NTT) and the inverse NTT (INTT). The FBU is a small-area and low-power auxiliary block prepared for potential scenarios that the main fast NTT/INTT processor is not fully functional. While the fast NTT/INTT processor aims to provide all NTT/INTT bins efficiently, the FBU specializes in calculating only one of the bins in a more efficient manner than the fast NTT/INTT processor. Hence, it can be particularly useful in evaluating few erroneous bins on behalf of the malfunctioning main processor. To this end, we first leverage the recurrence relation of the Goertzel algorithm, which has been used to efficiently compute a single bin of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and tailor it for the NTT/INTT based on the analogy of the transforms. Moreover, we hybridize it with another recurrence relation of Horner’s rule to maximize the efficiency regardless of which bin is being evaluated. Furthermore, the datapath of the FBU is designed to minimize both area and power consumption. More specifically, a modular adder and a modular subtractor are unified into one, and a modular multiplier is dynamically deactivated by isolating operands when unnecessary. With minimal operators, then, the FBU can evaluate any of the NTT/INTT bins for the positive-wrapped convolution (PWC) as well as for the negative-wrapped convolution (NWC). Implemented in a 65-nm CMOS process for CRYSTALS-Kyber, CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon-512, and Falcon-1024, the FBU occupies only 11% area, and consumes only 9% power of the single-path fast NTT/INTT counterparts on average. To highlight and promote the system-level usefulness of the FBU, an efficient dual modular redundancy (DMR) for the NTT/INTT with the FBUs is additionally proposed. By analyzing the patterns of error propagation in the signal flow graph, we substitute multiple stages of the complicated fast NTT processor with the lightweight FBUs, without compromising the detection coverage. Instead of discarding the whole frame, the FBUs may recompute only erroneous bins and the main processor may save power. The current design of the FBU assumes a serial interface, and is most compatible with the single-path fast NTT/INTT.

item.title: CT-LNN: FPGA-Based Accelerator for Continuous-Time Liquid Neural Networks
item.description: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) based on multivariate time-series data is a representative edge intelligence workload. However, conventional deep neural networks, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), suffer from limited FPGA efficiency due to sequential dependencies, irregular memory access patterns, and large model sizes. This paper presents an end-to-end FPGA acceleration framework for Liquid Neural Network (LNN)-based real-time HAR. By exploiting closed-form continuous-time dynamics, the proposed approach enables parallel computation while preserving temporal modeling capability. Several algorithm–hardware co-design techniques are introduced to improve efficiency. An accuracy-aware power-of-two quantization scheme reduces bit width with a small accuracy loss, and a hardware-efficient activation approximation based on combinational logic eliminates transcendental operations. In addition, a contention-aware dataflow architecture with optimized multi-channel communication and hierarchical memory organization is developed. An optimized matrix–vector multiplication engine with 8-way cyclic banking is further implemented to enable conflict-free parallel access. The design is implemented on an Artix-7 FPGA and evaluated on the UCI ConfLongDemo_JSI dataset, achieving 94.34% accuracy with $688~\mu $ s latency and 15.12 GOPS throughput. The complete Zynq-7020 system consumes 1.81 W, including both the ARM Cortex-A9 processing system and the programmable logic, while the CT-LNN module on the PL side consumes 264 mW. Based on the total system power, the accelerator achieves 8.35 GOPS/W energy efficiency, demonstrating an efficient and scalable solution for edge deployment.

item.title: Scalable and Flexible Baseband Processor for 5G-A/6G Base Station
item.description: As an imperative part of supporting 5G-A/6G base station, baseband processor encounters more challenging key performance indicator requirements. The existing hardware designs for baseband processor have difficulty in achieving high flexibility, low latency and high throughput with high hardware and energy efficiency. We propose a baseband processor based on ASIP (Application Specific Instruction-set Processor) design philosophy and dynamic coarse-grained reconfigurable array (CGRA), which can enable flexible and scalable baseband processing operations in 5G-A/6G base station, and delivers three important merits: high throughput (56 Gb/s), low latency (0.9 ms) and high flexibility. Instruction fusion is a critical approach in ASIP to enhance computational performance and energy efficiency, we design dependency tracker and light-weight hardware resource table to eliminate data and structural hazards that arise from instruction fusion in ASIP, which utilizes low silicon costs to achieve performance improvements. Moreover, we propose parallel and conflict-free data addressing method with low storage overhead to minimize memory access latency. Fabricated in a 16 nm CMOS technology, our processor achieves high flexibility and high performance in supporting various baseband processing tasks and various MIMO scales for 5G-A/ 6G base station. Our processor achieves 889-10000Gb/s/W energy efficiency and 35-130 Gb/s/mm2 area efficiency for detection and decoding tasks, which are 1.2– $85\times $ and 2– $42.6\times $ those of state-of-the-art hardware designs respectively. To our knowledge, this is the first high flexible and high-performance baseband processor for 5G-A/ 6G base station.

item.title: Design and Implementation of a 32 × 32 MIMO Detector Based on Expectation Propagation Preprocessed Sphere Decoding
item.description: This paper presents a $32\times 32$ MIMO detector based on an expectation propagation preprocessed sphere decoder (EP-SD). At the algorithmic level, we propose reformulating expectation propagation (EP) statistics into an equivalent zero-forcing representation to serve as a preprocessing stage for sphere decoding. To further enhance performance with low complexity, a sorting strategy based on post-EP symbol variance and a fixed-enumeration scheme are integrated into the decoding framework. Regarding architectural innovations, we employ a second-order polynomial approximation for hardware-unfriendly operations, achieving a 99.7% area reduction in the statistics module. Additionally, a folded QR decomposition architecture and a clique-based buffer optimization are introduced, reducing the QR module area by 36.0%. The $32\times 32$ EP-SD was implemented in TSMC 40-nm CMOS technology, achieving a throughput of 1.99 Gbps at 331 MHz. Post-layout results demonstrate that the proposed design provides at least a 2.0 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement over existing hardware detectors while maintaining competitive normalized area and energy efficiency.

item.title: A Novel Flash-Based Finite Impulse Response (FFIR) Filter Featuring Processing In-Memory (PIM) for IoT Applications
item.description: In this paper, we present a novel mixed-signal flash-based Finite Impulse Response (FFIR) filter architecture for Internet of Things (IoT) applications. The FFIR filter is scalable in that it can implement any filter with up to a provisioned maximum number of taps. Our FFIR filter uses flash transistors, a type of non-volatile memory (NVM) device, to perform analog computations in the current domain, achieving low power, energy, and area requirements. We implement our design using a modified 3D flash architecture, which stacks flash transistors vertically, to reduce chip area. This design is well-suited for IoT applications and other scenarios where computational resources are highly constrained. Our FFIR filter consists of several Flash-based Coefficient Multipliers (FCMs). The FIR coefficients of each FCM are stored in its constituent flash transistors, with the threshold voltage ( $V_{t}$ ) of the flash transistors serving as a proxy for the filter coefficients. Furthermore, the impact of process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variations is mitigated by precisely tuning the $V_{t}$ of the flash transistors. The tuning of the $V_{t}$ of the flash transistors can be performed either in the factory by the manufacturer (to negate process variations), or by the user in the field (to negate voltage variations or aging effects). We evaluate the tolerance of FFIR filters to manufacturing variations through Monte Carlo analysis, demonstrating robustness to process and $V_{DD}$ variations. Our FFIR design achieves a significant improvement over previous approaches. Compared to Digital FIR (DFIR) filters operating at the fastest frequency (or the same frequency as our FFIR filter), the 2D implementation of our FFIR filter reduces the average power, energy, and area by $4.05\times $ , $1.95\times $ , and $2.27\times $ ( $2.25\times $ , $2.25\times $ , and $2.21\times $ ), respectively, while the 3D implementation achieves average area improvements of $2.64\times $ ( $2.57\times $ ). Our FFIR filters also achieve an average peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 38.01 dB and an average measured equivalent number of bits (MENOB) of 8.87 bits. In addition, we compare our FFIR filter with state-of-the-art Analog FIR (AFIR) filters as well. Our designs demonstrate significantly improved performance, achieving average reductions of $18\times $ , $32.9\times $ , and $194\times $ in energy per tap, area, and latency, respectively, compared with four recently published AFIR works. We also show that for our FFIR design, the use of 3D flash technology reduces the overall area by approximately 12.8% compared to the use of 2D (planar) flash.

item.title: Incremental Data-Driven Model Predictive Control for Offset-Free Output Voltage Regulation of DC--DC Converters
item.description: Standard data-driven model predictive control (MPC) schemes typically require a priori knowledge of the reference equilibrium input-output pair for reference tracking. However, in many practical applications such as DC–DC converter voltage control, the exact steady-state input is often difficult to determine due to system parameter uncertainties and load variations. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an incremental data-driven MPC framework for unknown linear systems. Leveraging behavioral systems theory, the framework predicts future trajectories via a purely data-driven parameterization and formulates the optimal control problem using input increments as decision variables. This formulation inherently incorporates integral action, enabling offset-free tracking that relies solely on the desired output. Consequently, it eliminates the need to pre-compute or estimate the corresponding steady-state input. Furthermore, theoretical analyses establish the recursive feasibility and exponential stability of the closed-loop system and ensure constraint satisfaction. Finally, experimental results on a DC–DC converter platform confirm the practical effectiveness and offset-free tracking performance of the proposed approach under various operating conditions.

item.title: Full-Stage Constrained Voltage Control of DC Microgrid Cluster With Uncertain ZIP Loads Over Unknown Network Topologies
item.description: To maintain voltage safety in DC microgrid clusters, existing constrained voltage control methods face difficulties in simultaneously handling full-stage operating conditions, load nonlinearities, and topology-induced network current uncertainties without accurate circuit and network models. This paper presents a decentralized nonlinear robust voltage controller for full-stage constrained voltage control of a DC microgrid cluster with uncertain constant impedance, constant current, and constant power (ZIP) loads over unknown network topologies. First, a projected voltage state is built through a link function and a barrier transformation. It embeds the unconstrained start-up stage, the transition stage, and the final voltage-constrained stage into a single state space, converting the irregular constrained regulation problem into bounded tracking in projected coordinates. The design relaxes the initial-state requirement of conventional barrier methods and avoids mode switching. Second, a nonlinear robust disturbance observer with a frozen-variable structure is developed to compensate for lumped ZIP-load and topology-induced network-current uncertainties without using current derivatives. Finally, a voltage controller is derived from the capacitor and inductor energy functions using only local voltage and current measurements. Lyapunov analysis proves constraint-preserving practical tracking, and DSP-based hardware-in-the-loop tests validate the constrained voltage response under reference changes, ZIP load variations, and plug-and-play events.

item.title: A Unified Loss Analysis Framework for Grid-Based Generalized Switched-Capacitor Topologies
item.description: Switched-capacitor converters (SCCs) are widely adopted in integrated circuits and increasingly used in data centers for their high power density and efficiency. A comprehensive analysis and selection of SCC topologies for a given conversion ratio is essential for high-efficiency design. Although grid-based synthesis methods enable the generation of numerous novel topologies, evaluating their losses still relies heavily on time-consuming simulations. This is because traditional theoretical analysis methods cannot be applied to “underdetermined topologies”, as their charge multiplier vectors cannot be uniquely determined by conventional methods. In this paper, we propose the dual-limit asymptotic current model and apply it to analyze underdetermined topologies, which constitute 96.61% of 4:1 SCC topologies. By constructing an analysis framework based on this model, we successfully achieved rapid analysis across the full topology space, with an analysis speed 235 times faster than the traditional parallel simulation. Theoretical analysis results were validated through simulations and prototype experiments, identifying several novel topologies that differ from conventional designs while demonstrating favorable efficiency under the evaluated parameter set.

item.title: Enhancement in Dynamic Performance of Multi-Converter Architecture
item.description: Operation of power converters with a common tie among input/output ports is a very established architecture in most of power electronics applications. However, interlinking operation of such layouts enhances analysis complexity. Moreover, considering inherent conjoin behavior, generic small-signal oriented tuning process becomes insistent. Thus, procurement of satisfactory dynamic response may not be guaranteed for substantial load perturbation as well as the formulation of control gain independently for each converter with this tuning process due to existing coupling interaction in operation. To analyze these concerns thoroughly and to figure out optimal possibilities, multiple converters forming a generic DC common bus layout are considered for investigation. To provide overall completeness to the study and to observe effect of feed-forward logic on system transfer functions, initially a small-signal based mathematical model is developed taking into effect of external ramp profile with/without current feed-forward information. Core insight showcased matrix correlation developed among parameters of various converters provides a major complexity in the loop-gain tuning process with such modeling approach. To deduce a simplified and independent tuning approach for individual power converters, trajectory-based large signal tuning approach is executed. Development of mathematical correlation for gain calculation and stability study is performed considering various transient events. A comparative analysis is carried out with the developed laboratory prototype for adopted control logic with different tuning approaches. Outcomes showcase improvement in dynamic performance of overall system with feed-forward logic as well as a simplified tuning approach with trajectory based method for multi-converter architecture.

item.title: Observer-Based Double Integral Output Voltage Controller for DC/DC Boost Converters With Triply Damped Performance Using Virtual Damping Injection
item.description: The proposed observer-based double-integral (DI) control technique precisely assigns a target triply damped transfer function to the closed-loop system while reducing the peak current level in model-plant mismatches and load variations. This study presents a few contributions: 1) a model-free low-pass filter-based observer that suppresses peak responses by filtering the output voltage measurement while simultaneously estimating its time derivative; 2) a simple observer-based output-feedback DI controller incorporating virtual damping terms to enhance closed-loop robustness with reduced reliance on an accurate power converter model; and 3) a performance recovery feature that reinstates the target triply damped input-output behavior through an order-reduction technique. The effectiveness of these contributions is demonstrated by experimental validation utilizing a 3-kW prototype DC/DC power converter integrated with a 32-bit digital signal processor.

item.title: Design of Broadband High-Efficiency Transistor-Based Rectifier Integrating Dual Continuous Class-F/F−1 Mode and Snow Geese Algorithm
item.description: This article presents the design of broadband high-efficiency transistor-based rectifiers, which combines continuous class-F and continuous class-F−1 with progressive phase shift. A design strategy of integrating dual continuous class-F and class-F−1 is proposed to release the limitation of single hybrid mode on working bandwidth. Then, a target impedance design space that satisfies the clockwise variation characteristic of impedance with frequency is proposed. After determining the target impedance, an intelligent optimization framework driven by the Snow Geese Algorithm is employed to achieve automated design optimization of the subsequent circuit topology. For validation, a broadband high-efficiency rectifier based on a GaN transistor is designed, fabricated, and tested. Experimental results demonstrate that the rectification efficiency between 61.9% and 87.3% is realized in the frequency range of 1.9-3.6 GHz when the dc load $R_{\mathrm {dc}}= 80~\Omega $ and the input power $P_{\mathrm {in}}=40$ dBm. The proposed rectifier has the widest operation bandwidth among traditional transistor-based rectifiers.

item.title: An Adaptive Sampling Frequency FOCV MPPT Based on Constant-Energy-Packet-Counting for Energy Harvesting Applications
item.description: This paper presents a high-efficiency buck-boost converter for thermoelectric generator (TEG) energy harvesting, addressing the demand for fast maximum power point tracking (MPPT) under widely varying input power conditions. The core contribution is an adaptive sampling frequency fractional open-circuit voltage (ASF-FOCV) MPPT scheme that significantly reduces sampling overhead. First, a constant-energy-packet-counting-based input power detection (CEPC-PD) module is introduced to monitor input power changes solely from switching signals with a negligible power overhead. This enables the proposed ASF-FOCV technique, which triggers an open-circuit voltage ( $\boldsymbol {V_{\textbf {OC}}}$ ) re-sampling only upon detecting a substantial input power change. To support this instantaneous sampling, a decoupled $\boldsymbol {V_{\textbf {OC}}}$ sample-and-hold (D-S&H) circuit is devised. This structure fundamentally breaks the classic trade-off in traditional FOCV between using a large sampling capacitor for long holding time and a small one for fast tracking. By decoupling the sampling and holding processes, the proposed D-S&H circuit achieves three key advantages: a short per-sampling open-circuit time of $1~\boldsymbol {\mu }$ s, an effectively infinite holding time, and the elimination of external voltage dividers or large capacitors. Compared to conventional fixed-sampling-frequency FOCV, the proposed ASF-FOCV MPPT maintains high tracking accuracy during steady state and achieves rapid response during transients. Experimental results demonstrate an MPPT efficiency exceeding 98% (99.5% peak) over an input power range of $50~\boldsymbol {\mu }$ W to 10 mW, a converter efficiency of over 80% (90% peak) across an input power range of $100~\boldsymbol {\mu }$ W to 10 mW, and minimum and average MPPT response times of $236~\boldsymbol {\mu }$ s and $544~\boldsymbol {\mu }$ s, respectively.

item.title: High-Efficiency Rectifiers With Wide Load Range Using Multiple Impedance Compression Networks
item.description: As a critical component for RF-to-DC conversion in RF electromagnetic wireless power transmission (WPT) systems, the RF rectifier significantly influences system performance. Traditionally, rectifiers are designed for specific loads at fixed frequencies and input power levels. However, even when the power-consuming devices remain the same in certain WPT scenarios, their equivalent load values may fluctuate due to varying operating conditions. High-efficiency rectifiers with a wide load range are proposed with multiple impedance compression networks (ICNs) in this paper. The proposed rectifiers are based on the conventional voltage doubler rectifier (VDR) configuration. First, our study shows that the load range of VDR is limited by circuit mismatch. Second, multiple impedance compression networks are used to address the mismatch problem and increase the load range. A detailed theoretical analysis is provided to explain the design methodology. Two rectifiers with different diode combinations are designed, fabricated, and tested for validation. The first design produces an RF-to-DC efficiency higher than 50% for a load range from 0.09 to 10.5 k $\Omega $ at an input power of 20 dBm. The second design achieves over 50% efficiency for a load range between 0.4 and 21.7 k $\Omega $ under an input power of 6 dBm. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in extending the load range. A comparison with existing works shows that the two rectifiers achieve the widest load range for both low and high input power levels.

item.title: Shuffle-CIM-NR: From Shuffle-Based All-Analog Inference to Noise-Resilient Charge-Domain Computing-in-Memory for Near-Sensor Intelligence
item.description: Near-sensor smart sensing requires compact and energy-efficient hardware to support local deep neural network (DNN) inference under stringent power, latency, and accuracy constraints. Analog compute-in-memory (ACIM) exploits analog-domain multiply-accumulate (MAC) to improve computing density and energy efficiency, making it a promising hardware solution for low-power near-sensor smart sensing. However, existing ACIM architectures still suffer from two major limitations for near-sensor deployment: the power and latency overhead caused by cross-bank partial-sum (pSUM) accumulation and digital-domain non-MAC operations, and the computation accuracy degradation induced by analog circuit non-idealities. This brief presents Shuffle-CIM-NR, a shuffle-based charge-domain CIM architecture for low-power and robust near-sensor inference. By mapping shuffled convolution groups into individual CIM banks, Shuffle-CIM-NR eliminates cross-bank pSUM accumulation and enables one-shot 4-bit signed-weight/activation MAC operations. To further improve analog computing robustness, Shuffle-CIM-NR co-optimizes the activation input path, signed multi-bit MAC computation, and analog readout, while integrating batch-normalization (BN), activation, and quantization into the ADC. Implemented in TSMC 22-nm CMOS, the proposed architecture achieves an energy efficiency of 283.2 TOPS/W and an area efficiency of 2.73 TOPS/mm2 with excellent linearity, providing an efficient and robust CIM solution for near-sensor smart sensing applications.

item.title: A 6T--11T In-Memory Computing Architecture for Near-Sensor Pipelined Binary Neural Network
item.description: This brief presents the fabrication and experimental validation of an interlaced 6T-11T CMOS in-memory computing circuit designed for low-silicon-area pipelined binary neural networks. The circuit implements a weight-stationary architecture in which input activation values are sequentially stored in 6T SRAM columns, while 11T cells retain the convolution weights and perform binary XNOR-based multiply-and-accumulate operations, naturally aligning with the column-parallel readout topology of CMOS image sensors. The circuit has been fabricated in a 180 nm standard CMOS process and experimentally characterized. Measured results on a binary convolutional layer demonstrate operation at 1 MHz with a simulation-assisted energy efficiency of 18.53 TOPS/W. The interlaced organization embeds the line-buffer functionality required for streamed convolution within the IMC array itself, so that image rows are processed as they are read out from the sensor.

item.title: A Heterogeneously Integrated Balanced Doherty Power Amplifier With Reconfigurable Adaptive Bias for 5G-Advanced Power Class 1 Terminals
item.description: This paper presents a heterogeneously integrated balanced voltage-combined Doherty power amplifier (DPA) for 5G-Advanced n77 power class 1 terminals. A reconfigurable adaptive bias technique is employed in the peaking amplifier to enhance broadband linearity. In addition, a compact transformer-based quadrature coupler is developed as the input splitter and output combiner, realizing an area-efficient balanced architecture with inherent load mismatch resilience. The fabricated DPA operates from 3.3 to 4.2 GHz and achieves more than 39 dBm saturated output power over a 24% fractional bandwidth while occupying only 1.27 mm2 of GaAs HBT area. Under a 100-MHz 5G NR signal, it delivers 34 dBm linear output power with power-added efficiency (PAE) exceeding 40% and adjacent channel leakage ratio (ACLR) better than −40 dBc without digital predistortion.

item.title: A Frequency-Reconfigurable Single-Stage Analog Linearizer for Joint AM–AM and AM–PM Compensation in Wideband PAs
item.description: Conventional analog predistortion techniques typically address amplitude and phase nonlinearity separately, often incurring a narrow operating frequency range. This brief presents a frequency-reconfigurable single-stage analog linearizer (SSAL) that jointly compensates for both amplitude and phase nonlinearities over a broad frequency coverage, using only a single transformer. The SSAL integrates diode-connected transistors with a nonlinear inductor, enabling simultaneous amplitude-to-amplitude (AM-AM) and amplitude-to-phase (AM-PM) correction in a compact circuitry. Moreover, the switchable transistor arrays are introduced to extend the operating frequency range and enhance linearization performance. Prototyped in 65-nm CMOS with a wideband PA, the proposed SSAL shows significant linearity improvement over a broad frequency range. The measurements reveal that the output power at $P_{\text {1dB}}$ (OP1dB) is improved by 3.4/3.9/3.1 dB to 16.6/17.8/16.5 dBm and the power added efficiency (PAE) at $P_{\text {1dB}}$ is increased by 9.5/12.8/8.9% to 22.1/28.8/22.5% at 25/30/35 GHz. The error vector magnitude (EVM) is decreased from 6.9/7.1/7.1% to 3.4/3.4/3.4% at 27/30/33 GHz under a 400 MHz 256-QAM OFDM signal.

item.title: Automated Synthesis of Multi-Frequency MMIC Matching Networks via Neural Dynamic Programming
item.description: This brief presents a neural dynamic programming (NDP) framework for the automated synthesis of MMIC matching networks. Given complex source and load impedances over multiple frequency points, we formulate the synthesis objective as maximizing the product of the transducer power gains ( $\boldsymbol {G_{\textbf {T}}}$ ) of the matching network, or equivalently, the sum of $\boldsymbol {G_{\textbf {T}}}$ in dB. To address the combinatorial optimization arising from multi-element cascaded topologies, the synthesis is reformulated as a dynamic programming problem. A sequence of neural networks is trained to recursively synthesize the matching network with one element at a time. The proposed NDP framework is implemented in a commercial GaAs process and validated through a set of four-element matching-network synthesis experiments. Compared with a genetic algorithm, the proposed method achieves an average improvement of 0.74 dB in $\boldsymbol {G_{\textbf {T}}}$ product while reducing the synthesis time from 35 s to 0.5 s.

item.title: Energy-Efficient Approximate Multipliers Based on Error-Compensating Approximate Adders
item.description: This work presents energy-efficient approximate multipliers based on two complementary types of approximate adders, one that underestimates and another that overestimates the result of addition. Owing to their simplified logic structures, these adders significantly reduce hardware cost. The main strength of the proposed approach lies in exploiting the complementary error behavior of these adders. When strategically placed within the partial product reduction stage of an approximate multiplier, their opposing error tendencies enable effective error compensation, resulting in a favorable balance between accuracy and hardware efficiency. Applying these adders to 8–11 least significant columns of an 8-bit multiplier yields substantial hardware improvements, including up to 53% reduction in delay, 82% reduction in energy consumption, and 76% reduction in area, while maintaining mean relative error distance (MRED) values between 3.4% and 12.1%. For similar accuracy levels, the proposed multipliers consistently outperform state-of-the-art approximate multipliers in terms of delay, power, and area. The architecture is scalable, allowing larger bit-width multipliers to be constructed iteratively from smaller configurations, with increasing hardware benefits observed at higher bit-widths for comparable normalized error levels. This work further evaluates the proposed multipliers in practical applications, including deep neural networks and image processing. When integrated into the fine-tuned ViT-Small vision transformer model, the design incurs only a 0.1% reduction in classification accuracy while achieving 37% energy and 40% area savings compared to an exact multiplier. Image multiplication and Sobel edge detection experiments also demonstrate high output quality, with PSNR and SSIM values exceeding 30 dB and 0.9, respectively.

item.title: An Energy-Efficient Sparse MobileNetV1 FPGA Accelerator With Chained Depthwise Separable Convolution and Computation-Aware Pruning
item.description: MobileNet has been widely adopted in mobile applications due to its lightweight architecture based on depthwise separable convolution (DSC). However, developing an efficient MobileNet accelerator remains hard as the DSC consists of two heterogeneous operations, depthwise convolution (DWC) and pointwise convolution (PWC). In addition, workload ratios between the DWC and PWC vary across the DSC layers, causing workload imbalance and thus underutilization in the accelerator. Pruning that removes unimportant weights worsens this problem as sparsity is not evenly distributed. In this brief, we propose an energy-efficient FPGA-based accelerator for sparse MobileNet with a novel operation called chained depthwise separable convolution (CDSC) and computation-aware pruning (CAP). The CDSC reformulates the consecutive DWC and PWC operations as a single operation, which resolves the underutilization problem by making a fixed workload ratio between the DWC and PWC in all DSC layers. Furthermore, the CDSC combines sparsities of the DWC and PWC, and this chained sparsity significantly reduces the computations of the CDSC-based MobileNet. To maximize the effect of the chained sparsity without significant accuracy loss, the CAP iteratively searches for efficient pruning targets by simultaneously considering the accuracy and the number of computations. The proposed accelerator is implemented on the Xilinx ZCU104 FPGA platform, and achieves the best trade-off between the accuracy and energy efficiency.

item.title: A 93.7% Peak Efficiency Compact Reconfigurable Switched-Capacitor DC–DC Converter With Soft VCR Transition
item.description: This brief proposes a compact reconfigurable switched-capacitor (SC) DC-DC converter targeting the miniaturization trend of Internet of Things (IoT) devices and dynamic voltage scaling (DVS) applications. The proposed topology utilizes only 21 switches and three flying capacitors (CFLY) to achieve step-down voltage conversion ratios (VCR) of 5:4/3/2/1, converting a 1.5 V input to a 0.16–1.19 V output. A soft VCR transition technique is employed to eliminate the hard-charging loss of the $C_{\mathrm {FLY}}$ , while an all-NMOS switch implementation is adopted to minimize switching losses. Fabricated in a 180 nm CMOS process, the converter achieves a measured steady-state peak power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 93.7%, supporting a maximum output current of 240 mA. Under periodic VCR transitions at 100 kHz, an average conversion efficiency as high as 85% is attained.

item.title: Distributed Data-Driven Dynamic Event-Triggered Control of Power Buffers in DC Microgrids
item.description: Direct current (DC) microgrids have attracted increasing attention due to their high efficiency and compatibility with renewable sources and energy storage systems. However, existing cooperative and communication-efficient control schemes for power buffers still rely heavily on accurate system models, which may limit performance under parameter variations and topology changes. This brief develops a distributed data-driven dynamic event-triggered control framework for power buffers in DC microgrids. Historical state-input trajectories are used to characterize the interconnected system and synthesize the controller directly, thereby avoiding explicit model identification. A dynamic event-triggered mechanism (DETM) is introduced to reduce unnecessary transmissions, and a model-free co-design of structured feedback gains and triggering weights is established via Lyapunov theory, the S-procedure, and linear matrix inequalities (LMIs). The design is centralized offline but distributed online: stacked trajectories are used only for LMI synthesis, while the implemented law follows the prescribed communication sparsity. Simulation results show that the proposed method achieves fast energy and voltage regulation under load disturbances while reducing communication burden compared with model-based and periodic communication strategies. Additional robustness discussions are included for representative parameter-perturbation and topology-change cases.

item.title: Two-MOSFETs-Based Memristor Emulator for Ultrahigh-Frequency Signal Processing
item.description: This article proposes a novel memristor emulator design capable of operating in the ultrahigh-frequency (UHF) range. The proposed memristor emulator, implemented using two nMOS transistors and a grounded MOS capacitor, is designed and simulated in the Analog Design Environment of Cadence Virtuoso using a 90-nm CMOS technology. It achieves a maximum operating frequency of 3 GHz, with a power consumption of 13.52 $\mu $ W. The robustness of the proposed memristor emulator is validated through extensive simulations, including temperature variations, process corners, capacitance variations, and different combinations. In addition, short-term nonvolatility analysis has been conducted to evaluate its memory characteristics. The layout of the proposed memristor emulator is presented, along with prelayout and postlayout simulations. Furthermore, hardware validation has been performed using commercial ICs (IRF840). Applications such as an 8:3 encoder, an adaptive neural network, and a ring oscillator circuit using the proposed memristor emulator are also reported in this article. The simulation results confirm that the memristive encoder functions correctly at 2 GHz and the ring oscillator generates an oscillation frequency greater than 2 GHz, demonstrating the emulator’s suitability for UHF applications.

item.title: ANP-Flow: A System-Level Simulation and Performance Prediction Toolchain for Asynchronous Neuromorphic Hardware Enabling Co-Exploration
item.description: Energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware with ultralow power consumption is increasingly promising for edge–artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Most digital neuromorphic hardware is designed with asynchronous circuits as they naturally match the sparsity and event-driven features of neuromorphic computing. However, designing asynchronous neuromorphic hardware faces challenges, including a lack of system-level hardware simulators and performance prediction methods, making it difficult for designers to explore the nonnumeric architecture design space of asynchronous neuromorphic hardware and find an optimal architecture that meets the demands for various edge computing scenarios. In this article, we put forward asynchronous neural processor (ANP)-Flow, a toolchain for asynchronous neuromorphic hardware including system-level simulation, performance prediction, and algorithm–hardware co-exploration. The key innovations include: 1) a fully asynchronous, highly concurrent system-level simulator is developed for the first time, enabling fast simulations for asynchronous neuromorphic hardware; 2) a novel graph neural network (GNN)-based hardware latency prediction model and a residual network (ResNet)-based power consumption prediction model are presented for asynchronous neuromorphic hardware. Experimental results show that they, respectively, achieve over 0.9 of average $R_{2}$ score and less than 2% of mean average percentage error (MAPE) rate on datasets with various network scales, traffic patterns, and process nodes; and 3) an algorithm–hardware co-exploration framework is proposed, improving energy-delay product of asynchronous neuromorphic hardware design by 1.8 times compared with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) work. To the best of our knowledge, ANP-Flow is the first end-to-end asynchronous neuromorphic toolchain with an integrated framework from circuit to algorithm, enabling joint algorithm–hardware design space co-exploration.

item.title: Device Endurance-Aware Adaptive Layer Selection for DNN Training on IMC-Based 2.5-D Systems
item.description: Deep neural network (DNN) training is both a compute- and memory-intensive operation. There exist several techniques that make training faster and more energy-efficient on state-of-the-art (SOTA) von-Neumann architectures. Resistive random access memory (RRAM)-based in-memory computing (IMC) together with 2.5-D technology delivers an energy-efficient solution to execute DNN training. However, due to the low endurance of RRAM devices, a limited number of weight updates can be performed. Therefore, in this work, we propose an adaptive layer selection approach for DNN training to improve the lifetime of a 2.5-D system with RRAM-based IMC devices. Specifically, during training, DNN layers are adaptively selected for weight updates at each epoch based on their importance to overall training accuracy and their energy–delay product (EDP) information. Thorough experimental evaluations on the proposed IMC-based 2.5-D system with different DNNs show 19% improvement in the EDP on average, with only 0.5% loss in accuracy when compared to the SOTA technique, where all layers are trained. Moreover, on average, our proposed technique improves the device lifetime by up to 15% with respect to the SOTA approach.

item.title: RoboPIM: A ReRAM-Based Accelerator for LLM-Based Robotics Applications via Dynamic Task Slicing
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant potential in improving robotics applications through natural language processing capabilities. Matrix multiplication dominates the computational workload in these LLM-based robotics systems, and resistive random access memory (ReRAM) provides notable performance benefits due to its inherent parallelism and energy efficiency. However, matrix multiplications in these applications pose dual heterogeneity challenges, encompassing both structural and scale heterogeneity. Structurally, these applications involve both standard dense matrix operations and block-structured sparse multiplications, where sparsity patterns vary significantly with robot topology. In terms of scale, matrix sizes range from just a few to thousands of dimensions, making large ReRAM crossbars designed for LLM inefficient for small-scale robotics computations. Existing acceleration approaches fail to address this dual heterogeneity, limiting their effectiveness for LLM-based robotics applications. In this work, we propose robotics applications-processing in memory (RoboPIM), the first low-energy ReRAM-based accelerator tailored for LLM-based robotics applications. robotics applications-processing in memory (RoboPIM) adapts to the diverse matrix multiplication requirements across robot platforms and LLM configurations. Our design features a ReRAM architecture with various crossbar sizes and implements a dynamic task slicing scheme that allocates matrix slices to appropriately sized crossbars. To maximize ReRAM’s parallel processing capabilities, we develop a two-stage scheduling strategy that efficiently manages matrix multiplications while enhancing hardware utilization. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that RoboPIM achieves $2.85\times $ and $6.85\times $ speedup across diverse robotic platforms and LLMs, respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art domain-specific solutions.

item.title: A High-Density RRAM Memory Architecture With IO-Assisted-Core-Transistor 1T1R Array and Two-Level Encoding for Edge AI Models
item.description: The deployment of AI on edge devices requires high-capacity on-chip memory to mitigate the performance and energy overhead of frequent off-chip data movement. Resistive random access memory (RRAM) has emerged as a promising candidate owing to its nonvolatility, high storage density, and low read cost. However, its adoption faces several challenges, including reliability concerns at high density, insufficient scalability for increasingly large AI models, and lower access frequency compared to CMOS-based units. In this work, we present a high-density and reliable RRAM memory architecture enabled by algorithm–hardware co-design. On the hardware side, a 1T1R array leveraging small core-voltage transistors for density and peripheral IO transistors for program reliability is introduced, together with a 16-step tunable current source for robust readout. On the algorithm side, a two-level encoding scheme is proposed to compress AI model storage with low implementation cost, while a burst-mode read strategy alleviates the frequency disparity with CMOS processors. Our experiments show a storage density of 17.4 MB/mm2 @ 28 nm, with $1.23\times $ to $4.15\times $ compression rate, $4.99\times $ read-out energy reduction compared to SRAM baseline, and $4\times $ higher read frequency. System-level evaluation further confirms the performance and efficiency improvements of the proposed design.

item.title: Beyond Uniform Approximation: Toward Efficient Computing in Logarithmic Number System for Large Language Models
item.description: Logarithmic number system (LNS) offers a more efficient quantization format than the integer system for data in large language models (LLMs), with inherently simple implementation for multiplication operations. However, the addition operation in LNS is relatively complex and difficult to balance between precision and hardware overhead. In this work, we observe that the input patterns of the computing units in the inference phase of LLMs exhibit highly skewed frequencies, resulting in nonuniform contributions to the final error. Based on this observation, we propose the beyond uniform approximation (BUA) to enhance the efficiency of LNS additions. From the perspective of lookup tables (LUTs), we propose LUT reshaping to efficiently reduce the approximation error, as well as LUT trimming, a heuristic method for simplifying LUTs within a given error budget. From the perspective of the entire LNS adder, we introduce auxiliary circuit approximation (ACA), which further reduces the hardware cost by simplifying computing data paths that are less frequently activated. Together, these techniques enable efficient approximate computing in LNS. Experimental results indicate that, compared to the multiply accumulate (MAC) unit using the naive LNS adder, BUA significantly reduces perplexity across various LLMs while reducing area-delay product (ADP) by 26.7% and power-delay product (PDP) by 30.8%. Compared to the traditional integer MAC unit, LNS with BUA achieves higher zero-shot accuracy while reducing ADP by 35.1% and PDP by 44.0%. Moreover, we also offer additional approximation options that provide greater hardware savings with only minor degradation in accuracy.

item.title: Simulation-Guided Approximate Logic Synthesis Under the Maximum Error Constraint
item.description: Approximate computing is an effective computing paradigm for improving the energy efficiency of error-tolerant applications. Approximate logic synthesis (ALS) is an automatic process to generate approximate circuits with reduced area, delay, and power while satisfying user-specified error constraints. This article focuses on ALS under the maximum error constraint. As an essential error metric that provides a worst case error guarantee, the maximum error is crucial for many applications such as image processing and machine learning. This work proposes an efficient simulation-guided ALS flow that handles this constraint. It utilizes logic simulation to: 1) prune local approximate changes (LACs) with large errors that violate the error constraint and 2) accelerate the SAT-based LAC selection process. Furthermore, to enhance scalability, our ALS flow iteratively selects a set of promising LACs satisfying the error constraint to improve the efficiency. The experimental results show that compared with the state-of-the-art method, our ALS flow accelerates by $30.6\times $ and further reduces the circuit area and delay by 18.2% and 4.9%, respectively. Notably, our flow scales to large EPFL benchmarks with up to 38 540 nodes, which remain challenging for existing ALS methods tackling the maximum error constraint.
